titulo: The Best 2-in-1 Convertible Laptops of 2025
transcricao: Two-in-ones are unique category of laptop that allows you to type at a desk one second and carry it around as a tablet next. We often see them favored by artists, students, and business users who want to take notes with a pen or draw. Today, we're going to be going over which two-in-ones we think are the best for which users. If you want to see more options than what we discussed today, check out our website bestlaptop.deals. You'll find a best two-in-one list there, and you can also track sales there to make sure you're getting the best deals. Now, if you plan to use the pen capabilities on these laptops, you'll be happy to know that almost all modern two-in-ones, and definitely all the ones on this list, support Microsoft Pen Protocol 2.0. It allows for over 4,000 pressure levels and tilt. This means you can bring your own pen if you already have one that is compatible with that protocol. This is especially nice considering they do not always include the pen in the box by default. Make sure to double-check this before you buy as some of them may be included in a package deal from the manufacturer, but not from the store. Okay, let's get started. Best budget two-in-one, OmniBook 5 Flip. The OmniBook 5 Flip is the best new budget two-in-one that we've seen and one of the only ones drops to around $400. With its metal chassis, we feel it's better built than other super cheap laptops like Lenovo's IdeaPad 1 or 3 and nicer than Dell's lowest end line. It doesn't have much else that's unique besides the price and its two-in-one capabilities, but the price alone is a big selling point. Its keyboard is pretty comfortable, its mechanical trackpad is fine enough, it has a good selection of fast ports, and it has a 1920 by 1200 IPS screen with mediocre color accuracy, but that's acceptable at this price point. The experience using HP's standard rechargeable pen is smooth with a little resistance. The tip of their pen has a spring in it, which is unique to other manufacturers. It makes it feel similar to writing on a pad of paper. The pen magnetizes to the chassis pretty firmly, which is convenient, and it also comes with two exchangeable tips. The laptop's cons are that it's a bit heavy for its size, which is not ideal in tablet mode. It also gets warm while charging, and it only has 8 gigs of RAM in the cheapest model. Before you choose to upgrade just for more RAM, we'd recommend the next one on our list. It can often be found for around the same price as the upgraded OmniBook and is a much better laptop. Best value two-in-one, Yoga 7. For those of you who want a high-quality two-in-one that is well under $1,000, Lenovo's Yoga 7 or 7i 14 both have a lot to offer. A very comfortable keyboard, a nice OLED screen with better color accuracy, Wi-Fi 7, and a good port selection, all of which are rare in the price range. It just feels better built than other laptops that it competes with. For ports, some of their speeds depend on whether you get the Intel or AMD model. Watch our full review for details linked below. You still get a USB-C port on either side, an HDMI port, and USB-A port, all nice to see in this small form factor. Using the Yoga Pen from Lenovo, the experience was solid, and we felt it was smoother than on HP's model with less resistance. We tend to find the pen experience on two-in-ones either lean smooth and silky like this one or more paper-like like the HPs. Whether you like the smoother style is up to you, of course, but Josh and I prefer it. Some of its cons are that it looks quite plain in the gray color and is also a bit heavy for this form factor. Overall, if you want better CPU performance and faster ports, we recommend the AMD model. If you want better graphics performance and battery life, go for the Intel, particularly the Core Ultra 7 model. That has the better integrated GPU. Both are a great buy when found around $800. Some alternatives in the value range include the HP OmniBook X or 7 Flips and the Dell Plus two-in-ones. We feel these both are not as well built, their keyboards aren't as comfortable, and they are a bit heavier than the Yoga 7s. They also don't last as long on battery. Another alternative that we found in the price range was this Dell Pro two-in-one currently on clearance selling for around $700. We feel this one is likely better built since it's from their business range, but we weren't able to get it in to test its screen or weight because stock is limited. Might be worth checking out though when it's on such a good sale. Best premium two-in-one, Yoga 9i. Next, the Yoga 9i two-in-one is a super premium laptop that can frequently be found on sale. Its good build quality, immersive speakers, bright high-resolution OLED screen, and super comfortable keyboard are all a standout in the two-in-one category. Even though we as a team felt the Yoga 9i is the winner, Josh prefers the OmniBook Ultra Flip, which is our close runner-up. The Flip has a little better battery life, a haptic trackpad, and is a bit more compact and portable. However, its keyboard feels low travel, so it isn't as comfortable, its screen doesn't get as bright, and its speakers aren't as good. Funny enough, we like the Yoga 9i just as much as we did last year, and the chassis hasn't changed. In fact, its CPU performance was better last year, and battery life was around the same, so you might as well buy that one, especially if it's cheaper. The last positive on this laptop is that we like the pen experience on it more than on the OmniBook. It glided easier by comparison and felt more comfortable to write notes on. We'd really only recommend the OmniBook over the Yoga 9i if you want the most compact 14-inch two-in-one. Another premium alternative to the Yoga 9i, also by Lenovo, is their ThinkPad X1 two-in-one. This one does have the option of a haptic trackpad by default, as well as great battery life, solid build quality, and a slightly better keyboard. If you're a fan of the red trackpoint, it's the only option in this video that features one. We feel its cons are that it is a bit heavier and its coating feels a little cheap, not to mention it's expensive for what it is, which is common for ThinkPads. We think the Yoga 9i is much more premium feeling than this one, but if you're looking for the best battery life on our list, this is the one to get instead. Just be aware it performs pretty poorly on battery, so it's only suitable for basic tasks unplugged. Best creator two-in-one, ProArt PX13. If you're using your two-in-one for some video editing or Photoshop work on the go, the Asus ProArt is a fantastic choice. It feels premium and well built, has a stunning 2.8K OLED screen with great color accuracy, it's super portable at only 13.3 inches, and it features a dedicated graphics card up to a 4060. It's the only one on our list that has one. Because of this, it performs the best in creative tasks like Premiere Pro. Also, thanks to its Ryzen 9 processor, it's much more powerful than the other ones we've mentioned, which you can see in our Cinebench benchmark. Despite its better performance, heat and fan noise is minimal in light use. Fan noise only gets loud during performance tasks, and the middle keyboard deck also warms up a bit. The pen experience on the ProArt has always been quite silky to me with excellent palm rejection. Plus, it's nice that the Asus pen comes with different nibs for creatives. The major cons on this laptop are that it has poor battery life, its screen is locked to a 60 Hz refresh rate, and it's expensive. The screen is especially disappointing for gamers who may have loved this laptop otherwise. Overall, it is one of a kind and has been my favorite product I've reviewed since I started working here, but it's not for everyone. Because of its size, it has a smaller screen, which may be less useful, and it doesn't have enough room to properly cool its high-performance CPU and GPU. I think if you're considering this one, I would personally wait until CES when we might be getting a refreshed version that will fix some of its flaws, or check out our best gaming two-in-one that comes next, also from Asus. Starlink is SpaceX's answer to providing global, high-speed internet coverage, using a network of thousands of satellites buzzing around the planet in a region known as low Earth orbit. While Starlink may be a business unit within the broader SpaceX company, it's seen as crucial to its overall goals of making humanity multi-planetary and exploring bodies like the Moon and Mars. SpaceX launched its first batch of Starlink satellites back in 2019, and since then, adoption of the service has ballooned. Starlink now has over 2 million active customers and is available on all seven continents and in over 60 countries. Starlink has been praised for its ability to connect remote parts of the world that would otherwise not have access to reliable internet. With around 5,000 active satellites now in orbit, Starlink satellites account for the majority of all the world's active satellites. This growth is uncharacteristic in the sense of its magnitude. Whereas prior satellite service providers have ramped up to anywhere at most between 500,000 to a little bit over a million subscribers, and this has taken, you know, a ten year period, Starlink's race to 2 million subscribers has taken only the better part of two years. By design, LEO satellite constellations like Starlink are more flexible than geostationary satellite networks like those operated by legacy satellite internet service providers Viasat and HughesNet. These satellite service providers have been constrained on capacity. They launch large geostationary satellites the size of a mini bus weighing multiple tons, and they last 15 years. So what ends up happening is they have more boom, bust cycles than Starlink, who tends to introduce capacity so far at an unrelenting pace, so they're able to onboard more and more subscribers by continually launching new satellites. Production was initially estimated to be as high as $3,000 per unit. At the time, SpaceX charged consumers $499 for its equipment, meaning the company was eating a lot of the cost, since SpaceX has cut the manufacturing cost of its antenna to under $600 and charges residential customers $599 to buy them. Starlink's ease of use and deployment has made it an indispensable tool in the Russia-Ukraine war. The big benefit of Starlink and how it's being used in Ukraine today, it is communications. Here's Musk reflecting on Starlink's importance at the 2023 Viva Technology conference in Paris. Russia had actually taken out all of the satellite communications and all of the ground communications, except for Starlink. It was the only one that was still operating, and even today, it is still the only one that is effective at the front lines. And Starlink today is the backbone of the Ukrainian military communications. One of the other benefits that we're seeing in Ukraine from the use of Starlink is its overall resilience. With thousands of satellites on orbit at any given time, it makes it a lot harder to jam all of those satellites or to target them all. The other benefit just how agile and quickly they can move. Questions about Starlink's and Elon Musk's outsized influence on the war came to a head when it was revealed that in September 2022, the SpaceX CEO had refused a request by Ukrainian military officials to turn on Starlink service in Crimea, which would have allowed for a sneak drone attack on a Russian naval fleet. In June 2023, the Department of Defense did sign a contract with SpaceX for its use of Starlink in Ukraine. SpaceX has also won a Department of Defense contract worth up to $70 million to make a military-specific version of Starlink called Starshield. Seeing the influence Musk's Starlink may have on geopolitical matters has prompted some countries to invest in their own satellite networks. The European Union has said that it will contribute €2.4 billion to help build out a constellation that's expected to reach full capacity by 2027. China is building out its own low Earth orbit satellite internet network, after the country made it clear that it didn't want Starlink services being offered to its citizens. Taiwan, wary of Musk's ties to China through his other venture, Tesla, too, has expressed interest in a proprietary satellite network to help shield the country from a potential assault from China. SpaceX has said that it eventually wants to launch as many as 42,000 Starlink satellites into orbit. Competitors including Amazon, Eutelsat OneWeb and Telesat want to launch thousands more satellites. And that's not even counting the several nations planning their own megaconstellations. The concern of the astronomical community is mainly due to the fact that these satellites are very numerous. We are moving from the 2,200 satellite of two, three years ago in orbit to something that will be 40,000 or even 100,000 satellites. So for most of the time during the night, these satellite are illuminated by the sun. And so they are visible in the sky and they interfere with the observation, in particular with photographs that the astronomers take for their research. This image, taken from a telescope in Chile in November 2019, illustrates the concerns from astronomers. The telescope, meant to see images of distant stars and galaxies, instead captured the light trails of 19 Starlink satellites. Observations from the Hubble Space Telescope, long lauded as a vital research tool for astronomers, have also been affected. Benvenuti says SpaceX has been responsive to concerns from the scientific community. He points to several design changes SpaceX made to its satellites to reduce their brightness, but says more needs to be done. The final solution is to know exactly, for every satellite, the precise position in the sky at any time from any observer. And so we are working with the companies to have this information and create a service that can be used by any observer, and they will know when the satellite is crossing their field of view, and they can plan their observation in a way that this disturbance is avoided. Satellites also pose a threat to radio astronomy. The interference to the radio observation is a very serious one and very difficult one, because this satellite are there to transmit information toward the ground in microwaves. So the only solution is to switch off the transmission when the satellite is in view of one of the large radio observatory. So what we are trying to do now is to negotiate with the company, to have the switch off the transmission when they are over these facilities. The report went on to say that by 2035, if Starlink satellites did not fully burn up in the atmosphere before falling back to Earth as designed, the FAA expects one person on the planet to be killed or injured every two years as a result of Starlink satellite debris. The pace of growth that Starlink has exhibited will be difficult for them to keep up going forward, and for a couple of reasons. titulo: Framework Just Made Their Best Laptop Yet
transcricao: I want to start this video by thanking Framework for flying me out to their event in San Francisco. They put me up in a nice hotel and fed me yummy food. That being said, their hospitality did not sway my opinions on their announcements. Let's start with the star of the show, a brand new version of their Framework 13, the 13 Pro. The Framework 13 Pro is bringing us a refined CNC aluminum chassis. It comes in black, aka graphite, which looks quite sharp. Silver looks a little dated in my opinion, even on something like the MacBook Pros, and the black feels more modern. The new color does pick up fingerprints pretty badly, so it's still available in silver if you prefer that. The new chassis feels a bit more premium and well-built, but the difference was not as big as I was expecting. The size and form factor itself couldn't change too much because they've made it backwards and forwards compatible. All the displays fit in both chassis, old mainboards can go in the new chassis and vice versa. On the keyboard, there is now an alternate colorway, as Framework calls it, with gray and orange accent keys on their black keyboard. I love this. It truly makes it look like a laptop that belongs to a coder. On the other hand, they have a lavender accent option, too, which I expected to like more, but I think the white text on the lighter lavender keys makes them hard to read. Another big announcement on this new 13 Pro is that we are getting a brighter 2.8K touchscreen option. This not only helps small text look sharper with its high resolution, but also adds functionality we did not have previously. It's rare that we see a matte, non-reflective display that also supports touch. As with the prior screens, 13.5 inches with a 3x2 aspect ratio, which provides more vertical space than many modern laptops. Still, it's disappointing that it's an IPS panel, not an OLED or tandem OLED. Instead of the screen, the crowd was more excited by the haptic touchpad. >> We know that touchpads are where Windows and Linux laptops have typically fallen behind MacBook Pro, so we put a ton of focus on this. Framework's mechanical trackpad might be one of the better ones I've used, but finally having a haptic option is great. I got to try the touchpad, and I think the tap-to-click was a bit too sensitive. I found myself double-clicking a little, but tracking felt smooth. Hopefully, on a production unit with some minor settings changes, it would be fine. In terms of overall quality and premium feel, this laptop is nicer than it used to be, but not as nice as something like Lenovo's Yoga Slim 7i Ultra. That is the most premium laptop I've ever used. The Framework 13 Pro simply isn't at that level, but I'd say it's getting to the level of other metal laptops, like the Samsung Galaxy Book 6 Pro. Now, while these improvements are great, the new Intel processors are just as exciting. All three CPU options offer benefits that we haven't seen in prior Framework 13s. To help you figure out how these perform, I'll be showing you some example laptops with these chips. First, you've got the higher-end 16-core X CPUs, which offer solid performance rivaling Apple's M5 base chip, but definitely not at the level of an M5 Pro chip, both of which can be found around this price point. They've also included a 100-W charger to support these new 16-core Panther Lake chips. The 8-core CPU falls near the bottom here, but it lasts forever on battery, which is probably where Framework's 20-hour battery life claim is coming from. Of course, we'll have to test that and see what it actually gets because they test video playback, and we don't feel that's very realistic. We do office tasks instead, and likely at higher brightness, which is closer to what we think someone would actually do unplugged. We should still be seeing much better battery life than last gen, though, especially since they've included a larger 74-W battery instead of the 61. This new one is still compact enough to fit in the same space as the smaller one, though. Lastly, back on the CPU options, both higher-end X chips bring awesome integrated GPU performance, similar to an entry-level dedicated GPU. I often use X chip laptops for light creative work, like reviewing our videos at lower resolutions, and they do a good job of that. Another improvement to the internals is the 13 Pro's LP-CAM memory modules. These can offer fast memory speeds comparable to soldered RAM while still being replaceable. This technology is super cool. We're glad to see Framework is the first to truly embrace it here. But, let's talk about where the team and I were a little disappointed. There is still a single-fan cooling solution. Panther Lake is more efficient than prior chips, yes, but I still think we're going to want two fans with those more powerful X CPUs. A more effective cooling solution means less fan noise under heavy load and a cooler-feeling laptop. I imagine this decision was made because of compatibility, but I do hope they find a way around it soon. We'll have to wait and see how it does under load, so get subscribed with the notification bell on so you can see our full review when it drops. We'll test all of its performance modes to see which has the best balance between performance, heat, and fan noise. Okay, now for the rest of the announcements. The Framework 16 is getting a facelift, or I guess you could say they're filling in the cracks. One of the biggest complaints about the Framework 16 is how its modular design around the keyboard and trackpad makes it look janky and sometimes even cheap. The pieces moved around a bit when you touch them, so I'm glad to see a new haptic touchpad that comes on a singular plate, which looks much cleaner and more cohesive. The part housing the keyboard will also have a single-plate option. Both of these make the laptop look much better, but it's still a clunky laptop. Another new product for the Framework 16 is this new Oculink dev kit where you can use an external GPU directly via eight PCIe lanes. This avoids the bandwidth issues of other external GPUs that connect via USBC or Thunderbolt. With this dev kit, you can either connect to a Framework GPU module or a desktop GPU. We're actually testing quite a few external GPUs right now for a big video on them. I'll add this one to our list. The last product they went over was their new wireless touchpad keyboard, which I will admit looks a lot like a product I already have in my home. We use ours for the living room PC we game on and connecting to our servers. If you also have one, you might know they can be a bit janky and don't always work perfectly. If this thing can improve on those even a little bit, it'll be great. Regardless, it will get Framework in front of more people, which is a good thing. Another product they announced is their new laptop bag for the 12-in and 13-in Frameworks. The black one looks fine, pretty boring, whatever, but the silver one, which I think they're going for like a spacesuit look, really just ends up looking like duct tape. I did not like it, and I think it looks cheap. All right, let's wrap. We like what we're seeing here a lot. In the past, Framework laptops didn't make sense for most people outside of techie land. The modularity doesn't matter to everyone, the laptops can look sort of Frankenstein, and the chassis weren't very stylish. Plus, they were just too expensive. This pricing often negated the whole value proposition of an upgradeable laptop. What's the point of a Framework if it's cheaper to just buy a regular laptop, sell it every 3 years, and get a new one? But, now we are seeing Framework address this. Firstly, the Framework 13 Pro looks and feels more premium. Nice enough that I'm willing to recommend it to more mainstream users. It's now more competitively priced. We are seeing laptops with X chips go for well north of the $2,000 this one costs, and they don't offer the repairability and upgradeability of a Framework. Also, there has never been a better time to use Linux instead of Windows. We are delighted that Framework is doubling down on their commitment to support Linux, too. Windows laptops are just getting way too expensive, as I said, and Windows itself is getting worse. Who wants Copilot and advertisements constantly shoved down their throat? Back on Framework, one product Josh mentioned he would love to see is a thin and light with a larger screen. He and I feel that many developers prefer a larger screen to work off of while maintaining portability that the Framework 16 doesn't give you. Anyways, that's everything we've got on this announcement. Make sure to get subscribed with the notification bell on because we'll absolutely be reviewing the 13 Pro when it comes in and putting it through our rigorous testing suite. Thanks for watching, and I hope you all have a wonderful rest of your day.

out should I keep it or not you see this device is a true Marvel of engineering there are just so many great things about it yet for the life of me I can't work out what use case this computer is actually ideal for so today I'm just going to tell you what I love about the Surface Pro and then the concerns that I have with it let's start with a good the device itself feels extremely wellb built and it looks stunning especially in the sapphire blue color my model has the X Elite chip with the OLED display 16 gig of memory and 512 gig of storage I can tell you that this thing is fast all my displaying fan noise and heat you feel but they are irrelevant with this device even when the laptop's processor is maxed out during cinebench on its highest performance mode the fan noise was quieter than the air conditioning in our office there was just nothing to measure and in real world use it was dead silent when it comes to the heat you feel the device itself does get noticeably warm however the way I and most people use it will be with your hands on the keyboard cover so you never feel the warmth anyway the display is stunning it is a fast refresh rate high resolution OLED panel text looks super crisp and it gets very bright although I wouldn't say bright enough for comfortable outdoor use particularly as the display is glossy and a bit reflective that being said you don't notice this at all in indoor use because it's high brightness combats the reflections the speakers are surprisingly good they have a nice clear sound that gets loud enough and just doesn't seem lacking for a small device like this one also I was delighted to see the cover around the back that allows you to easily access and upgrade the SSD now I bought the Surface Pro with the new Surface Flex keyboard cover which includes the slim pen it is extremely convenient to use you can use it wirelessly away from the main device the keyboard cover charges the moment it is connected the pen is kept neatly out of the way and the cover itself where it charges wirelessly yet the moment you pick up the pen it connects and just works the whole thing is just so seamless Bravo Microsoft now when it comes to the keyboard as an actual keyboard it is fantastic for what it is there is minimal deck Flex key travel is solid with a satisfying click and the keys have three stages of backlighting the trackpad is larger than in Prior years and extremely accurate look I don't normally use a pen when operating a laptop that is but this one was so good that even I ended up using it here's how the webcam looks and sounds on the Surface Pro it is a high quality one but it is very wide so as you can clearly see the Surface Pro 13 is truly an amazing piece of tech well why the hell did I do the Josh thing and say something negative I.E I couldn't figure out who should buy it well the reason is for the majority of users unfortunately there just seems to be better options out there let me explain what I mean say you're using this device for productivity work general office applications web browsing and that sort of thing for these tasks it certainly works well enough but compared to a laptop using it just feels cramped for starters it's screen is a small 13-in panel this doesn't seem that much smaller than the 13.8 in of the surface laptop 7 but in real use it is even factoring in it's 3x2 aspect ratio which does allow you to see more content going down the page I still just didn't see all that much and far fewer lines of text than what I saw on my Surface laptop 7 if you think you can alleviate this by flipping the device into a portrait mode you can't its kickstand doesn't support that orientation it would have been really nice if Microsoft angled the sides of the kickstand so you could do that one other issue with small screen devices like this one is that they aren't great for your back you tend to hunch over as you use them anyway it wasn't just the display that felt cramped and a little uncomfortable it was also the keyboard cover there is no Palm rest so when typing on it either you end up holding your palms above the device or you have to bend your wrist to match the angle that the keyboard deck is slanted at both of which I found tiring and a little uncomfortable now you can detach the keyboard and use it wirelessly in front of the device laying it flat on a table and that certainly helps but now the screen is pushed back further away from your eyes so you may have to zoom in to compensate and that means you're seeing even less content than before and on the trackpad while larger than pry ones it still isn't as large as the surface laptop sevs I found myself occasionally running out of vertical room there are also some PM rejection issues which are annoying a few times while using this device the cursor just jumped to a random spot on on the display in all fairness this does seem to be a very common issue on Windows laptops with half trackpads I can't believe in 2024 apple is still the only company to perfect a trackpad anyway this device also limits you to where you can use it desks tables and other flat surfaces only I like to use my laptop on the couch this is 100% noggo for this device it becomes a balancing act to keep it from toppling over now using the Surface Pro as a replacement for a laptop obviously isn't what makes it so special it's how versatile it is it's a touchscreen tablet with excellent pen support that can run the full catalog of Windows applications that last Point application support has been a key advantage of buying this device over its most obvious competitor the iPad iPad OS has severely limited applications available as I said earlier this year's Surface Pro uses one of Qualcomm Snapdragon processors this brings with it many advantages but because it runs the arm version of Windows Windows several specialist applications just don't run natively that means they run slower or don't work at all look I still think the surface pro has much stronger application support than an iPad but this competitive Advantage is now Slimmer continuing with the comparison to an iPad Pro the Surface Pro is significantly heavier this makes it far less comfortable when holding it and using it as a tablet your arms will tie very quickly now we haven't talked about battery life yet and it's important we do Qualcomm has spent monstrous amounts of money paying YouTubers to Hype up these devices one of their main claims is how good their battery life is many are saying all day battery life or that you no longer have to think about charging we are independent of these campaigns and let me tell you battery life on this device is not good for general office work and web browsing with minimal background applications open I struggled to get more than 5 hours this was on full brightness on the recommended performance mode where I was mostly continuously using this device if I had walked away more often and allowed the screen to shut off or even turn down the brightness it would likely have lasted longer but that's just not how I use my laptops I was so disappointed with its battery life I tried it a second day same result look this device's battery isn't the largest its screen is high resolution and bright so that affects things but this is kind of in line with what we are seeing on all these Qualcomm laptops they deliver incrementally better battery life than Intel and amd's older chips but they are so certainly not at MacBook levels that being said I'm not dissing Qualcomm here either the fan noise on their laptops is significantly less than the windows ones that came before them so overall they are a step forward to finish off with my cons on the Surface Pro the display does suffer from a screen door effect which means when you're looking at like colored content which you do a lot of when working on office documents you can clearly see colored dots poking through this is a common problem on OLED displays particularly ones with touchscreens there is a cheaper Surface Pro by the way with an IPS panel I don't have that model so can't comment on that one but I do have the surface laptop 7 with its IPS panel and this issue is less noticeable also on the ol display the color gamut isn't wide enough for professional color work we found this Odd as notbook check reported a much wider color gamut than us and yes we changed the relevant settings and Microsoft have implemented very granular brightness levels if you lightly press the brightness up and down button it only changes the brightness a microscopic amount which is extremely annoying lastly it would have been convenient to have at least one usba port my wireless mouse still uses a usba receiver and that matters because the trackpad does have occasional P rejection issues like I said let's end talking about pricing to get the model that I have we'll set you back $1,500 to add on the all important Flex titulo: Framework 13 Core Ultra Review
transcricao: framework is a new laptop company that burst onto the scene around 3 years ago their claim to fame is that their laptops are fully upgradable and they have excellent Linux support well they have finally come out with a version of their framework 13 with Intel's core Ultra processor for those who love what framework brings to the table this version is incrementally better there are improvements in power efficiency heat and fan noise but you might be surprised to learn that you aren't getting a huge boost in performance over their previous Intel version or one at all when compared to to their framework 13 with AMD zen4 now if you're an average laptop buyer just interested in whether you can get an upgradeable laptop that's on par in terms of overall quality with the latest from other manufacturers unfortunately you'll be underwhelmed in geekbench which tests a variety of common performance tasks this new framework outperforms both its previous versions with AMD and Intel in cinch however which tests the laptop when performance is maxed out it performs worse than the older framework with AMD zen4 we were skeptical of these results so we reran the test again and confirmed our data was still accurate with the most recent Windows updates compared to the performance of other competing laptops around this price point it's simply uncompetitive when looking at Power draw you can see why framework only feeds at a Max of around 45 Watts but it averages down to 30 Watts under continuous load this Max is a little lower than prior models although the average is unchanged at this power draw this Intel processor just isn't competitive especially compared to those of other manufacturers moving on to integrated Graphics that is where the core Ultra chip in this laptop does improve over prior Generations in time spy it scores better than the other Frameworks despite its CPU doing worse and the same goes for wildlife extreme but it still performs worse than many competing laptops now under these demanding loads the CPU doesn't get that hot at 77° C this is likely because it's not fed that much power unfortunately even though they've kept the CPU itself cooler you still notice some heat when using the device in light use the right palm rest warmth is particularly noticeable I found it tolerable but Josh and Taylor found it distracting and uncomfortable this may be due to The laptop's Limited cooling from its single fan design there is good news with the fan noise though with the stepup decor Ultra the laptop was dead silent during light tasks and quieter than prior Generations under Max load one upgrade you may want is framework's new Fast refresh rate display it gives you 2.8k resolution which upgrades you from 200 PPI to over 250 and allows you to avoid fractional scaling in Linux it also gives you 500 nits of brightness and slightly increased color accuracy best of all it UPS your refresh rate to 120 HZ this is is a much needed update one disappointing thing is that this isn't an option if you simply buy their pre-built core Ultra from the website personally I'm going to want the device to arrive ready to use even if I value upgradeability so it's frustrating that I don't have that option if I want the better screen as a whole the laptop looks almost identical to Prior Generations in that it looks boring the only new visual stylings are that you can get colored bezels and USBC ports I think the red is kind of cool but they appear as a bit of an afterthought and rather Frank and steiny the device simply does not feel as premium as competing laptops in this price point there is also some screen and keyboard deck Flex the positives are that it is portable at just under 3 lb and its charger is Tiny the aluminum finish is also fingerprint resistant the keyboard which is the same as prior Generations is one of the nicest I have used on a laptop I would even call the typing experience enjoyable it has ample key travel and a completely standard layout it doesn't replace the right control key with the co-pilot key like most modern Windows laptops I definitely like this Josh feels that the key is good but has kind of slipped down the rankings with other new keyboards that have come out the trackpad also seems to be the same as prior versions it is fine for a mechanical one but about middle of the pack that being said it isn't as accurate as trackpads on devices at this price point like the surface or MacBook Air now let's take a quick moment to show you how the speakers sound on the [Applause] framework we find the speakers to be pretty BL shallow and overall unpleasant this lines up with previous generations on the other hand the port selection on this laptop is definitely one of the best and most Innovative parts of the framework laptop other than the included headphone jack framework uses a customizable expansion card design this means that there are four card slots that you can utilize in whatever way works best for you and thanks to it being an Intel device all four of these ports are Thunderbolt capable from a newly available fast SD card reader to 2.5 gig Ethernet or display Port Gen 2 there are so many ways that you can customize these ports to fit your needs you can also order extra to swap them out this is surely one of the coolest things about the laptop as far as connectivity goes it comes with Wi-Fi 6E as with everything in these laptops the Wi-Fi card is replaceable but it would have been nice if it came with Wi-Fi 7 just to speak on upgradability for a second the whole thing is upgradable only one screw type is used it comes with the tool in the box and there are detailed instructions online it's as easy as it's going to get and framework dominates in this category now let's go over battery life for our results we tested with both the newer and the older screens to provide the most comprehensive data on battery the laptop's performance is dropped fairly significantly after a 30-minute cinebench test on the older screen the framework ends up with 69% battery remaining on the newer screen 73% tomato tomato for lighter use shown by our Netflix test it had 74% remaining with the older screen and 60% with the newer one this shows us that the new screen is definitely having a negative effect on battery life the version we initially received cost around $1,500 and that has the older screen if you wanted to build it yourself with the new screen and SD card reader it will cost you 1,750 and this brings me to my main point of concern with these laptops for an average buyer their cost is so high for what is unfortunately a poorer performing chip in an outdated chassis for a similar price you could get a much more powerful laptop with dedicated graphics like the Asus sairus G14 or Pro px13 or if you just want something lightweight that's premium a similarly speced MacBook Air for someone though who truly demands an upgradeable laptop though or wants excellent Linux support the framework is unique and it can't be beat and as we've shown you this year's update does bring you incremental improvements you now have access to a better screen and other things like a fast SD card reader which is certainly unique in a laptop this size as an aside framework is a smaller company and they have done amazing to achieve what they have one word of advice though that I'd give them after having reviewed that framework 16 which was a little disappointing is less is more maybe if they hadn't diverted resources to titulo: Snapdragon X2 Is FAST… But Should You Buy It?
transcricao: The review you've all been waiting for, the Zenbook A14 and A16 with Qualcomm's new Snapdragon X2 chips. The Zenbook A16 with the Elite Extreme processor gives you great CPU performance both unplugged and plugged in. It's got a beautiful 16-in touchscreen and decent battery life for a somewhat reasonable price, especially when you consider it comes with 48 gigs of RAM. The A14 is the 14-in version and is a bit cheaper while still giving you class-leading CPU performance. Its screen isn't as good, but its battery life is better. This all being said, these are Qualcomm laptops that run the ARM version of Windows. We did a big deep dive where we tested a ton of different professional apps where we found that more run than when these X chips were first released 2 years ago, but there are still some that don't run and others that don't run well, particularly when you factor in the middling performance of these chips' integrated GPUs. To cut a long story short, we feel the A16 is a very good laptop for most software developers. The A14 is a good laptop for a programmer who maybe doesn't care about the screen as much. If you are just buying one of these for basic use though, these are hard to recommend over Apple's MacBook Airs. Those deliver a better all-round experience for most users and they're cheaper. If you want to buy any of the laptops we discussed today, we've linked them down below as well as several other alternatives. Or you can check out our website bestlaptop.deals. We track prices right across retailers to show you whether they are actually a good deal. Now, let's get into the meat and potatoes. These Zenbooks look unique, for sure. There is a speckled pattern to the lid that looks nice, but they are also the exact color of my grandmother's minivan growing up. This color is going to be very subjective. Some people can't stand beige and others think it looks refined. Personally, I do like the look of this laptop. It's just not as universally compatible with everyone's style as the silver Macbooks. For something more neutral, I would prefer the dark gray our ZenBook Duo came in. Colors aside, they have a smudge resistant coating over the whole chassis, which avoids pesky fingerprints. Both ZenBooks are super lightweight compared to other laptops in the same size class, which makes them a joy to bring with you, even the 16-in. But, there is a catch to the ZenBook's lighter weight and unusual coating. They lead to it feeling less premium than competitors who have aluminum chassis. Even though it's using a lighter metal, it's still well-built with minimal deck flex and screen flex. There is only a bit of give when pressing down on the lid, which you don't normally get with aluminum laptops. It doesn't even happen on the Neo, for example. The hinges on both ZenBooks are also reasonably stiff, but still able to be opened with one hand, and they have a nice little notch at the center to help you do so. Overall, we would consider these high-quality laptops for their price. Most of us here even think they feel pretty premium. They just don't compare to a MacBook. The display on the 16-in is much more noteworthy than the 14, so we'll start there. The A16 has a 16-in 2880 by 1800 OLED panel, which gets up to 500 nits of brightness and refreshes at up to 120 Hz. It's pixel density is over 200 PPI, which makes small text look super crisp for someone like a coder, who we think this laptop is great for. On top of that, it supports touch and pen, which would be good for some light creative work like Photoshop or Affinity, which I found it also does decently well. We didn't detect any screen door effect or noticeable PWM flickering, which means there are no quality concerns with this display. The only thing worth considering on the A16 screen would be the fact that it's glossy and doesn't quite get bright enough to combat reflections, particularly if you're outdoors or have bright lights behind you. The 14-in display, on the other hand, has a few cons. It's a 1920 by 1200 OLED panel that only refreshes at up to 60 Hz and goes up to around 400 nits of brightness. It is not a touchscreen, and we also detected some PWM flickering at lower brightness levels. The MacBook Air gives you a crisper, brighter display for the same money. Somewhere the Macs do not win out, however, is on the keyboard. The key travel on these ZenBooks is around 1.3 mm, which I find more enjoyable to use than the 1 mm Magic Keyboard on the Macs. There is a bit more resistance to the key press, and they are a bit more clicky. I tend to prefer that feedback. Josh likes quieter keyboards with less resistance. If you're looking for a quiet keyboard to sneakily type on during a meeting, this isn't it. Other than that, the layout is standard, and many people will be glad to see the keyboard on the 16-in is centered instead of including a num pad. On the trackpad, I think it's one of the better mechanical ones I've used. It has smooth tracking and an accurate click, although the click is a bit loud as well. Palm rejection seemed to work well in my experience on both the 14 and the 16, but that tends to be more of an issue on haptic trackpads. I would have rather seen one of those on both of these, but for mechanical ones, these are nice enough. Ports are another example of where the A16 takes things just a little further than the A14 to give you a bit more value. They both have two 40-gigabit USB-C ports on the left, also known as USB 4, then an HDMI 2.1 port and a headphone mic combo jack. On the right, they have a 10-gigabit USB-A port, but the A16 also gives you a fast SD card reader, which is a great addition. Unfortunately, neither of them offers charging on the right side. For speakers, I would say these laptops sounded pretty good. The bass was decent, and it only really got muddy around the higher registers. Take a listen. >> [music] [music] [music] [music] >> Here's how the 1080p webcam looks and sounds on the Zenbook A16, and it also has IR for Windows Hello. Here's how the 1080p webcam looks and sounds on the Zenbook A14 in studio lighting. We feel that both the A16 and A14 look a little oversaturated. Here's how the A16's webcam looks in normal lighting in my office. Still not great as far as the colors go. And here's how the A14 looks in normal lighting in my office. Now, if you've seen Josh's recent video on these Qualcomm X2 processors, you might have already seen how our A16 performs, but I'll still go over the highlights. The Zenbook A16 with the X2 Elite Extreme chip does phenomenally well in CPU tasks, pulling ahead of Windows competitors in terms of both single and multi-core. The Macs keep their crown in single core, but Qualcomm's results are still impressive. Core for core, we don't see the A16's chip beat out the much more expensive 18-core M5 Pro chip in Apple's 16-in MacBook Pro, but it beats similarly priced competition handedly. The A14 also performs very well, beating out modern Intel and AMD as well as the base M5 10-core, which is once again impressive for the price. If you're looking for CPU performance exclusively, both of these laptops are extremely compelling. When we look at how much power the A16 draws, it may seem like a lot at first, and it's certainly more than the MacBooks, but it is more efficient than Intel or AMD. The Zenbook A14 seems to be at a more optimal power level, though, since it gets 83% of the performance of the A16 with only 54% of the power draw. Which brings me to my next point. Likely because it draws more power, our Zenbook A16 gets quite warm in our CPU stress test. It also gets surprisingly loud. The A14 does a bit better here, but still not great. In actual use, Seth and I found both stayed much cooler and quieter than the Cinebench test would indicate. However, if you do plan to max out the CPU for an extended period of time, we'd caution you on the A16 specifically. Another option for a more comfortable experience is to run these laptops in their default performance mode. That standard mode on the A16, for example, performs at about 80% while drawing less power, staying quieter, and not getting quite as warm on the keyboard deck. 6,000 is still an incredible score for a laptop. For the A14, it's a very similar story in its default standard mode. You get most of the performance for less fan noise. Now, let's look at graphics performance. The new Qualcomm integrated GPU is a huge improvement from the original one. It is slightly faster when paired with the Elite Extreme chip in our A16. That being said, at this price point, there are far better options. If you go with Intel and AMD, you can get an Nvidia GPU. If you are sticking to integrated, Intel's X chip with its B390 is a bit faster, as is the M510 core. But, this isn't the full story. Many games and apps don't run natively on the ARM version of Windows. And even if they do, they aren't as optimized. For example, in Cyberpunk, Intel's integrated GPU pulls further ahead. You'll notice the MacBooks have the same problem as the Qualcomm chips here. These games aren't as optimized for those platforms. Seth and Josh tested a ton of games and apps for our other video I've mentioned, which I've linked below. League of Legends wouldn't install due to anti-cheat, and Marvel Rivals had some visual artifacts. So, if you're planning to do even casual gaming on the side, we'd recommend a laptop with a dedicated GPU at this price, or Panther Lake if you know your titles are lighter. Qualcomm is still a gamble for gamers. In creative tasks, it's better than gaming, but still a mixed bag. I took on the A16 one weekend and used it for publishing and photo editing work in Affinity, and it did great. I primarily used the Pixel and Layout apps. I don't recall any slowdowns or stutters for anything I was doing, and our Photoshop benchmark aligns with this. Not only that, but it never got too warm or loud, which made my photo editing sessions very comfortable. I also used it to review one of our videos back at the office, and it was usable. Some stuttery playback, but watchable at 1/2 resolution. Fan noise was a bit louder, but not obnoxious. Realistically, at the price point of the A16, an NVIDIA laptop is much better for video editing, as you can see in our graph. However, NVIDIA laptops have fan noise, and if you don't want that, Apple's MacBook Pro with M5 is still better than Qualcomm. When it comes to the Zenbook A14, it wasn't usable at all. Premiere fully freaked out and crashed due to OpenCL saying it was out of resources, even though I was only playing at a quarter resolution. It shouldn't be the fact that it only has 16 gigs of RAM, because we have played these videos back on other laptops that have that amount, but perhaps this is due to a lack of optimization. The A14 just wasn't usable for video editing. If you're looking for performance in other professional applications, including 3D work, engineering, and programming, check out that other video, but I'll summarize. We found these laptops are great for photo editing, like I said, and most programming. But, if you're using other professional apps, it's better to avoid these laptops unless you are absolutely certain what you're running will run and run well. For battery life, the A16 keeps up with the MacBook Pro 14 with the M5 Pro chip at about 9 hours, which is decent, but not as good as the one with the base M5. The A14 lasted longer at around 11 hours, only being beat out by the MacBook Pro 16, which has a much larger 100 Wh battery. This is a great result. Something else to consider here is how well the laptops both perform unplugged, which makes their battery results even more impressive. For Linux, we've seen some reports that Fedora 44 finally works on these Qualcomm laptops. You need to use the ARM version with some kernel runtime parameters, so we did this and still couldn't get it to boot at all. We also tried a custom Ubuntu ISO that has been confirmed to run on a few Snapdragon laptops, but we weren't able to boot there either. Linux still seems to be a no-go. As far as upgradeability goes, you can only really replace the full-sized M.2 SSD and the battery in these laptops. We were surprised to only see one slot in the 16, especially considering they had plenty of room. I feel like I've made my point. Qualcomm is absolutely heading in the right direction. The ZenBook A 16 in particular is very competitive at its price, particularly for coders. The A 14, less so. It has a smaller, lower resolution screen, which makes it more appealing for light users. But, if you are just looking at one of these for that kind of thing, we don't want to see you paying more for the incredible CPU performance if it won't benefit you. We'd recommend you just buy the MacBook Air, which is a more premium feeling laptop. It's around the same price and its CPU is plenty powerful. If either of the ZenBooks start to come with the lower-tier X Plus chips for less, our conclusions might change. So, check out our website for our latest recommendations. Thanks for watching and I hope you all have a wonderful rest of your day.

titulo: Why I Returned My MacBook Pro 16 (M3 Max)
transcricao: my new Macbook Pro 16 with the M3 Max chip cost me an eye watering $4,000 and it literally delivered zero benefits over my older M2 Max MacBook Pro 16 in fact not only did it deliver zero benefits but for my use case which for this laptop is video editing it ended up feeling warmer to the touch since video editing is such a common reason for people to buy one of these laptops I thought it was critical for me to get the word out there and share my personal experience so here's the background I've been using the MacBook Pro 16 with the upper end M2 Max chip and 32 G of memory to edit our videos on at least my portion of the edit as we do have two other editors here anyway my laptop has been really struggling I frequently get dropped frames when reviewing footage editing text is insanely laggy and rendering videos was taking way too long seriously sometimes it would take 20 minutes to render one of our videos and by the way often I render a single video multiple times that's because I share them with people to review and we find things that we'd like to change then of course we're render in multiple videos per week so all up I could be spending hours waiting by the way we do use Premier Pro and know we aren't going to be switching to deiny resolve anytime soon anyway as a professional YouTuber time is money so even if there is a modest performance increase by upgrading to the newest M3 Max version of this laptop it will be worth it for me plus buying a new laptop is a business expense and I get a pretty substantial tax break on it so netn net for me to upgrade makes more sense than it does for the average person and that's why it's even crazier that for the first time ever I won't be upgrading and instead I'll be returning this laptop back to Apple so let's double click in and I'll tell you what happened I chose the highest end M3 Max version of the MacBook Pro 16 because obviously I wanted the most powerful laptop that I could buy and I also knew it was the only one with a full 400 GB of memory bandwidth based on extensive prior testing I knew that memory bandwidth was critical for a laptop's performance when r rendering a video you can see an example of this on screen rendering a video on my MacBook Pro with the M2 Pro 12 core is substantially faster than rendering the exact same video on my newer M3 Pro MacBook Pro also with 12 cores the older M22 core has 200 GB per second of memory bandwidth whereas the newer M3 pro has less 150 GB Apple has nuked memory bandwidth in many of their latest laptops the reason rendering a video by the way is so dependent on memory bandwidth is that video editing is predominantly a hardware accelerated task and relies on Apple's media encoding engine that makes it a very fast operation so long as you have enough memory to store all the data you need and you have fast enough access to that memory please note the number of media engines also matters Apple's Max chips have two and the cheaper Pro chips only have one that is why professional video editors really must buy a Max chip in this laptop it will be up to twice as fast and yes this applies to all generations of Apple's M series of processors back on memory my M3 Max MacBook Pro 16 came with 48 gigs which I liked you see I was seeing some occasional yellow memory pressure warnings in activity monitor this means that I was running low on memory in my older 32 gig of memory M2 Max model so I wanted to triple check that it wasn't a lack of memory that was causing my performance issues when I say triple check I have tested this thoroughly before and in the past it just wasn't an issue in fact moving from 16 gig of memory to 32 gig actually made almost no difference for my specific video so knowing that the M3 Max chip has the same number of media engines as the M2 version the same memory bandwidth and that the amount of memory itself was unlikely to be a bottleneck no surprises as to what happened for video rendering the most intensive task that I do I saw no performance difference from paying $4,000 to move from the older M2 Max MacBook Pro 16 with 32 gig of memory to the newer M3 Max version with 48 this experience also reinforces something a lot of people overspend on memory on these MacBooks that's because they see the occasional yellow in the activity monitor and just like me think they need more you probably don't yellow means you may eventually need more memory red is what you actually have to be worried about that is the one that means you need more memory now anyway as there were no speed UPS in video rendering what about the other performance issues like Drop frames and the ludicrously laggy text editing yes the faster single core speeds of M3 did make those tasks a tiny bit faster you can see an example of our warp stabilizer results on screen but seriously if someone asked me to do a blind test between these two laptops I'm pretty confident that I couldn't tell you which was which they were just that close in their performance the only thing I did notice is that the M3 Max version felt warmer to the touch and you'd hear the fan spin up more frequently most likely because to get an M3 Max processor which I was forced to do to get the full 400 GB of memory bandwidth I now had to buy with a bunch of tech that I just don't need but will make the laptop feel warmer to the touch and this leads me to my conclusion whether a new laptop will be faster than an older one depends entirely on whether your specific tasks are actually using any of the new capabilities of that laptop in the case of these M3 processors the new capabilities that have been added really do very little for video editing yes they have significantly better 3D rendering they have R tracing and more performance CES but this just isn't where our slowdowns are and you're essentially paying more money for a bunch of stuff that you just don't need or want and I want to speak really personally here for a second I'm not immune to the feeling of missing out that Apple's marketing department generates around their new products even I have this sinking feeling like the M3 version just must be better and I'm missing out by sending it back but the reality is I'm not and all I'll be doing if I kept this laptop is giving Apple my money now before I close I do want to clarify one point what I discussed today was for video editors and those folks would be better off searching for an older M2 version of this laptop and just saving some money however if you're doing something that isn't as dependent on this kind of hydro acceleration say you're programming or just want a good all round laptop I do like the M3 pro version of these MacBook Pros the changes that Apple has made around the mix of cores and the more efficient cores are a net gain for you you get faster performance more battery life with even less heat you feel so I do recommend them but even still do not upgrade to an M3 MacBook Pro if you already own an M2 one if you are coming from an M1 model you probably will notice a little difference particularly in things like opening applications which will be snappier but you probably will still want to wait till the M4 versions on the other hand if you're coming from any intel laptop you will certainly notice a difference in battery life fan noise and heat you feel so go for the upgrade well that's all I got for you moral of the story ignore the marketing Hive and only spend your hard on Tech that will actually offer you a meaningful benefit if you like this video smash the like button and get subscribed not only does it help us grow this channel so that we can create more videos for you but it also makes my dearest mother very proud till next time go do something awesome with your day and I will catch you later

transcricao: all right we recently published a mega video comparing the absolute best 14-in laptops the moment we went live numerous people commented saying that I should have included the new slim Pro 7 with AMD also known as the yoga Pro 7 people were talking about this laptop like it was a breakthrough device a premium feeling product with an AMD processor and decent dedicated graphics all for a fairly affordable price well I've tested it thoroughly and I have to say I don't like this laptop today I'm going to show you why this laptop is totally overhyped and overrated and at the end I'll cover what you should probably buy instead to help demonstrate how average this laptop really is I'll be comparing it to its more expensive sibling the slim Pro 9i as well as many other major laptops around this price point let's get into it so this laptop comes with two variants the ryzen 7 7840 HS and the ryzen 7 7735 HS our one has the latter the 7735 HS and is the model sold at Best Buy now both these processors seem like they're from amd's current generation for high performance laptops but AMD has misleadingly named their processors the truth is hidden in the third digit of the naming scheme a three like in the model we have means the underlying Tech is actually from the older zen3 architecture from last year whereas the 7840 HS model is a real current generation zen4 processor we ran all our performance testing on both the default intelligent cooling mode as well as the Extreme Performance mode which you can configure from lenovo's Vantage software as you can see from geekbench which tests a variety of common performance tasks this laptop substantially underperforms the other laptops particularly in single core even the MacBook Air M2 a fanless laptop beat this one out it performed so badly that I was worried that perhaps its memory was only in jeel Channel mode and not quad but nope all good there and yes we ran the test multiple times with all drivers up to date let's now take a look at cinebench which tests how the laptop performs when under Max load it is still at the bottom of the pack in fact the only laptop to perform worse was Apple's M2 MacBook Air which as I said is a fanless laptop so its performance is heavily restricted due to thermals but that laptop benefits from no fan noise in fact since the slim Pro 7 performed so poorly let me add in the scores from lenovo's own yoga 9i that's a two-in-one laptop that is more targeted at casual users as you can see the yoga N I beat the slim Pro 7 quite substantially in single core and in multicore when on the default balance mode yes the slim Pro 7 is ahead by a good margin but when both were run on their performance modes it narrowed so even though it looks like this laptop has an HS processor which is supposed to indicate a high performing machine you really aren't getting that kind of performance it's not terrible performance but it's more at the Casual user level the good news though if I can call it that is since this laptop performs so poorly when you run it under a 10-minute torture test performance doesn't drop that much much which means the calling solution in this laptop is up to the task unlike the slim Pro 9i with Intel's 13th gen H series processor which has an identical chassis that laptop has to be throttled significantly for any long-running high performance tasks it still smashes this one though you can see in this test just how much better the newer zen4 AMD processor in the framework laptop does and same with the G14 which completely destroys this laptop in terms of performance by the way if you do get the Zen 4 version of this laptop the 7840 H S1 I wouldn't expect things to be all butterflies and rainbows the G14 will probably still perform better as it has a far beefier cooling solution as well as a faster ryzon 9 processor taking a look at Power drawer you can see that its average power drawer is more than the zen4 processor in the framework laptop which as you'd remember actually beat this one in performance but let's take a look at the all important performance per watt which is a measure of the processor's efficiency a more efficient processor means less heat to dissipate and therefore less fan noise you hear less heat you feel while using the the laptop and longer battery life as you can see this laptop's older zen3 processor has similar efficiency to Intel's current 13th gen it's really only when you run amd's new zen4 series with lower power that AMD becomes noticeably more power efficient than Intel and that's what framework is doing with their amdu series processor or of course if you buy an Apple laptop with an M series processor then that will also be efficient graphics performance let's talk about that RTX 3050 Graphics which is in this laptop for a sec honestly in 2023 an RTX 3050 is very low-end dedicated graphics heck the 3050 was a low-end dedicated graphics from last year and the current RTX 4000 series is definitely a big step up and also keep in mind that the integrated Graphics in AMD zen4 processors like the one in the 7840 HS Chip have really good integrated Graphics so an RTX 3050 is only a modest step up and isn't really going to get you into the Realms of playing current AAA games Hidden fan noise given this laptop's subpar performance you'd think the processor would run pretty cool it doesn't it runs hot and taking a look at heat you feel for performance tasks the laptop's keyboard deck does remain very cool to the touch which by the way is one of the strong points of this laptop but definitely do not put this laptop on your lap when doing anything intensive the underside gets very hot fan noise when Under full load is Extremely Loud under light use though like browsing the web or working on office documents the laptop again remains very cool to the touch this time also the underside in this use case the fans were almost always running but at a very low volume that I would consider almost in audible that being said the moment you do anything intensive like installing a program the fans will spin up battery life when on battery the performance of this laptop doesn't drop by much which is good that being said its performance is still at the back of the pack to test battery life for high performance tasks we ran cinebench on a loop for 30 minutes the laptop had only 40% battery remaining so don't do anything intensive on it while on battery for a more realistic test we dimmed the screen to 200 nits then played a Netflix movie on repeat over Wi-Fi for 4 hours at the end of The Run we had 50% remaining which is a decent score and should get you around 8 hours for this use case look and feel this laptop looks okay it's not a special or overly stylish looking laptop it does feel reasonably well built though however not at the Quality level of a Macbook one pro is the rounded edges which makes the laptop more comfortable to use in environments where you just don't have a lot of risk support like using it on a plane's tray table display the display is another weak point of this laptop on the surface there are some very good things about it it is large at 14.5 in it's got decent resolution and a fast 90 HZ refresh rate and it is a touchcreen but there are two serious issues with it firstly it just isn't that bright we measured around 350 nits which really is the minimum you'd want for indoor use on a laptop that costs north of $1,000 this isn't good and it really affects how much content you you can comfortably see on screen without needing to squint I found I had to run the laptop at a relatively High window scaling to make content large so it became readable this really negates the point of having a 14.5 in panel you can see how this plays out in my Excel test which shows how many rows I was comfortably able to see without needing to squint it was an abysmal 29 rows as you can see from my graph I was able to see more content on screen on laptops which have smaller displays the second issue is the displays colors they just AR aren't that accurate for a laptop with Pro in its name they're good enough for viewing content on screen just not for professional color work I mean heck my MacBook Air M1 which cost a fraction of the price of this one and came out 3 years ago has a brighter more color accurate display keyboard Lenova makes great keyboards and the one in this laptop is no exception it isn't quite at the heights of the slim Pro 9i which basically feels like you're typing on a mechanical one but it is extremely comfortable with an excellent tactile feel the trackpad is good enough but over overall cheapens the experience of this laptop tracking itself is pretty decent but the click feels just cheap and not 100% accurate the sound from the laptop speakers is awful they do get loud but the quality is atrocious it sounds tiny super processed and lacks Bas when we played the same track side by side with my MacBook Pro 14 Ethan even said it's like someone recorded the music from their MacBook on their phone then played it back using the phone speakers perhaps if your outlet is on the other side which may get in your way when it comes to overall portability it's not the most portable of devices you can see that the framework laptop is much lighter than this laptop here's the pricing in the USA the model that we have with the olda zen3 processor has a recommended price of $1,200 and the model with the new as zen4 processor cost just under $1,000 500 for that kind of money I don't like this laptop that's a decent chunk of change and what you're getting is a laptop that could be using a poor performing AMD processor that came out last year you're getting low end dedicated graphics also from last year you're getting a dim display with not the best colors and atrocious sound nothing about this laptop really says Pro as the name would imply and at the price range there are just other laptops that are so much better seriously when you have all these laptops side by side like we do it just becomes so obvious which are the standout ones and if you like this video you know what to do make sure to give us a like and get subscribed not only does it show your appreciation for the work we all put in but it makes my mother very proud till next vents towards the back of the laptop just make it look so cool and so does the RGB Keyboard Plus having the Lesser used ports around the back of the laptop make your whole setup just look clean at
