titulo: Schenker Vision 14 (ID4H1) Review - The 14inch Laptop You Should Buy
transcricao: tech family when it comes to laptops for most people i felt for quite some time the 14-inch form factor is where it's at these laptops are small enough to be portable but the screen is big enough to get some real work done particularly those with a 16 by 10 aspect ratio where you see a decent amount of information going down the page in fact when i think about buying a new laptop for myself the 14 inch form factor is the one i'd look for we've seen some really promising 14-inch laptops hit the market but all of them haven't really hit the mark for example the hp env14 is a powerful laptop but it's big and heavy the thinkpad carbon gen 9 is a quality feeling lightweight laptop with excellent battery life but its screen options aren't the best and its keyboard is less comfortable than thinkpad's evolved anyway i haven't found the perfect device for me luckily xmg reached out a brand i'd seen many positive reviews on my friends channels i was eager to try out one of their devices so jumped at the opportunity they asked me if i wanted to review one of their larger more powerful laptops but my audience contains a lot of students software developers and casual users plus i'm personally interested in a lightweight 14 inch laptop for myself so i thought their schenker vision 14 sounded more interesting and by the way sometimes i call them xmg shanku is actually their professional line and xmg they're gaming the vision 14 is really xmg's customized version of the tongfang id4h1 tongfeng is the manufacturer and assembler of the chassis and the core components you'll find this laptop customized and resold by a variety of brands around the world so over the last five weeks i've been using it and i have a lot to say about it as i was really impressed by this laptop let's start with the chassis it is extremely lightweight at only 1023 grams or 2.25 pounds when i think about which laptop i want to pick up and use on a daily basis and i have many one of the most important factors is how lightweight it is i want something comfortable to use on my lap and that isn't going to wipe me down in my backpack the good news continues as the build quality is much better than i expected it's got a full metal anodized aluminium chassis it isn't quite at the build quality of lenovo's thinkpad or delts xps line but it's better than dell's inspire online and as good as lenovo's ideapad line the laptop's lid has this satisfying click to it when it closes i'd assume it uses a magnet it does mean it's a little harder to open with one hand though the screen to body ratio of the laptop is excellent not a lot of wasted space from the bezel showing it looks modern and the logo on the front is very subtle the port selection is good you've got a thunderbolt 4.0 port on either side of the laptop that both supports charging which is great as you won't have to run a power cable around the back if your power outlet is on the other side which i have to do on a lot of laptops it has two usb a ports although these are the slower 3.2 gen 1 5 gigabit speeds there is an hdmi 2.0 port and an sd card reader the card sticks out a ton when it's in so make sure you don't accidentally hit it and break the card also the sd card reader is the slower uhs one type it's handy to transfer files in a pinch but it is not going to satisfy the needs of professional videographers or photographers transferring large amounts of footage internals are a welcome surprise you've got user replaceable ram and ssd yay what's awesome is xmg have spared no expense on their customization of this laptop you've got an extremely fast pcie 4.0 samsung 980 pro ssd it's called the fastest test scores of any ssd i've ever tested you've also got samsung ram you can see that the chassis has room for the dedicated rtx 3050 ti graphics that will be available in an upgraded configuration and there is room for a second cooling fan to call that the cooling solution with the one heat pipe does look a little lackluster it actually performs surprisingly well though which you'll see later in the video the display is excellent and exactly what i want in a 14 inch device it's got the perfect balance of pixel density display brightness and size for me to see a large amount of information with everything looking super crisp at a windows scaling setting that maximize the amount of information on screen without me feeling like i needed to squint i managed to see 44 rows of excel which is very satisfactory for this kind of device it's also a map display so even though it only has 370 nits of brightness the fact that it has no reflections on screen makes everything easy to see in most lighting conditions honestly it's plenty bright the colors are also good enough for most uses other than perhaps creating print material also the 90 hertz refresh rate makes scrolling feel very smooth only minor ding was there was a little backlight blade in a completely dark environment i would show you but it was quite minor and hard to pick up the keyboard is very comfortable to use ample key travel with a comfortable tactile click in fact the keyboard on this laptop is more comfortable than the latest thinkpad line honestly keyboard comfort is something that i see lacking in a lot of laptops these days i'm looking at you macbook pro however the keyboard's layout is also the biggest issue i have with this version of the laptop i'm used to an ansi keyboard layout xmg's version of this laptop only comes with an iso layout if you are unfamiliar with these two layouts the iso layout has a different shape enter and shift keys and the back and forward slashes are in different places ansi is heavily used in the usa and iso is used in other parts of the world no surprises due to the difference in layouts i made a ton of typing mistakes on this laptop's keyboard if you are used to an iso layout then this is not an issue at all but unfortunately at this time xmg does not offer a configuration with an ansi one you'll have to buy this laptop from another reseller of the tongfeng id4h1 chassis it's a pity as this is such a great laptop for me other than that one thing if you feel xmg should make an ansi version available make sure to tweet to xmg about it i'll leave a link in the description below the trackpad is good enough it's smooth and accurate for tracking however i found that when clicking it the trackpad depresses more than i'd like and accuracy during and after a click is not ideal it is perfectly usable though it's just not enjoyable now i kept performance to later in the review as my version of this laptop uses the well-known intel i7 1165g7 cpu i've been testing it for over a year now in many different laptops and i feel we all know how it performs the skinny is this it is plenty fast for everyday tasks like browsing the web watching movies and it's good enough for students it's also fast enough for light to medium weight coding and the g7 graphics is good enough for basic video editing and playing some simple non triple a games and of course esports titles but there are a couple of special things i want to call out which i noticed when i was running my tests on this laptop firstly xmg manages to keep this laptop running at 28 watts of power for an extended period of time which is really good for this cpu you can see how this plays out in my 10 minute torture test of cinebench r23 which tests how the laptop performs when the cpu is under full load you can see that this laptop annihilates every other laptop i've tested with this cpu the only exception is the hpn v14 i had the i5 version of this cpu by the way but that is a much bulkier and heavier laptop what is the icing on the cake is this laptop surface temperatures where you would have your hands remains very comfortable to the touch xmg have done a great job with this there is a trade-off as the fans run really loud when pushed like this by the way as i said i am testing the max performance of this laptop here on overboost mode for casual tasks like browsing the web the laptop remains virtually silent my dell xps 13 9310 runs noticeably warm into the touch and my hp spectre 14 has much louder fans during regular use like browsing the web writing code watching movies for these tasks this laptop remains cool to the touch and the fan noise is literally non-existent by the way xmg's configuration software is very cool it's one of the first i've seen that lets you limit the performance of the laptop based on how many decibels of fan noise you will hear very useful i ran a couple of gaming benchmarks and it didn't reach the heights of its cpu-only performance my hypothesis here is this laptop has a cooling solution that's good enough to cool the cpu but when we are also engaging the gpu it probably isn't robust enough and performance becomes limited i kind of wish they installed that second fan that the laptop has space for inside the chassis other than that wi-fi 6 performance is decent but latency mod results aren't great the laptop does have windows hello facial recognition which is handy oh and there is an included ethernet adapter that comes with the laptop the webcam is the usual garbage i mean this is the best possible lighting conditions right now and i mean look at the lamp behind me that's just not the right color the sound is surprisingly good even though speakers are downward facing the sound seems to travel very nicely through the chassis the speakers get loud and are relatively clear with a decent sound stage they do sound a bit tinny though and obviously there is pretty much no bass as small laptop speakers go though they are pretty decent just don't expect the full powerful sound you'd get on a macbook pro 13 here battery life the laptop has a 53 watt hour battery which is a decent size to test it i ran the laptop for five hours playing a netflix movie on repeat over wifi power mode was set to battery saver and brightness was set to about 75 percent which to be honest is still insanely bright on this screen eighty percent of power was used so it should be able to get around 6.5 hours operating like this but as i said the screen was still very bright i feel you should be able to hit close to eight hours if you dim the brightness a lot pricing xmg informs me that the price for my configuration is around 1 700 euros with windows pro so it definitely isn't a budget device it's more premium and that's how i'm going to judge it so here's what i think of the xmg vision 14. i like it in fact if there was a version of it with an ansi keyboard layout i'd probably buy one for myself and replace my dell xps 13. i like that it has a larger screen than the xps a more comfortable keyboard replaceable ram and it doesn't get as warm to the touch under regular use it also will be able to be configured with a powerful nvidia rtx 3050 ti graphics and xmg informs me there will be an option with intel's slightly more powerful h35 cpus for my use i like the laptop better than the hbn v14 as it's much lighter i like it better than the hp spectre 14 as it's quieter when it comes to fan noise compared to the new thinkpad range it has a more comfortable keyboard and an excellent matte display which i feel is better than the options available on say the carbon gen 9. it also has a more comfortable keyboard than the yoga slim 7 pro and the razer blade 14. so yes for my use case for a small laptop for browsing the web watching movies coding if you use an iso keyboard xmg's vision 14 is really good if you do want this laptop with an ansi keyboard try searching for other resellers of this tomfang chassis that being said if you're in the market for a device like this i still think there are a couple of other strong contenders depending on your use case if you're good with mac os the macbook pro 13 has better battery life better multi-core performance better speakers and a better webcam but its screen is smaller it's also a lot heavier and of course it doesn't have an option for powerful graphics the lenovo yoga slim7 pro with amd ryzen 5800h has a far more powerful cpu even though as i said its keyboard isn't as comfortable and it's heavier the thinkpad yoga is also a decent all-round option if you want to draw or take notes on the screen oh and of course the asus g14 has far more powerful components particularly if you want to do some serious a triple a gaming although to me it doesn't feel as quality of a device as this one and it's definitely bulkier well that's all for today folks xmg did leave a positive impression on me so i do plan to look at more of their laptops in future if you like this video you know what to do smash that subscribe button hit the thumbs up and the notification bell not only does it show your appreciation for the effort that goes into making these but it also makes my mum happy make sure to follow me on instagram twitter and tick tock for plenty of behind the scenes content and info on upcoming videos links in the description below till next time go do something awesome with your day and i will catch you later

titulo: ThinkPad X1 Carbon (Gen 9) vs X1 Titanium vs X1 Yoga vs X1 Nano Review
transcricao: Tech Family with me is Lenovo's new ThinkPad X1 range, including the Nano, the Titanium, the Carbon and the Yoga. I recently reviewed the X1 Nano, which I loved, and then the X1 Carbon. In fact, I had two of the X1 Carbons because I liked it so much that I was hoping to use it as my daily driver. So I wanted to see which was best, so I tried the Full HD Plus model with a Mi5 and then a 4K Plus model with a Mi7. But you guys kept requesting that I take a look at the new X1 Titanium. So I had Lenovo send that to me as well. And then since I have a habit of biting off more than I can chew, I was like, let's just compare and contrast all of them. So I got it in an X1 Yoga Gen 6 as well. Now normally in a video like this, I just say I value your time, so I'm just going to tell you up front, which is the best one. But in this case, it isn't clear. Each of these are good laptops with very different pros and cons. Actually, I will say that I'm not the huge fan of the Titanium. Anyway, there's no overall winner here, and heads up since I am comparing four laptops. I won't go into quite as much depth as I would for an individual review. But I'll definitely give you plenty of information to make and inform buying decision. And links to my four reviews of the laptops that I have done some for will be in the description below. And by the way, if you're new here, I'm Josh, and I buy and review a lot of laptops and talk tech from the perspective of what it's like to own and use these devices. If at the end of this video, you like what you watched, make sure to smash that subscribe button, hit the thumbs up and the notification bell. Not only does it show your appreciation for the insane amount of work that goes into making these heck, I just had an espresso to film this at 8 pm at night, so I'm pretty wired. But it also makes my mum happy. Let me give you a quick overview of these laptops. The Nano is the smallest and the lightest of the bunch, weighing less than £2 with a 13 inch 16 x 10 aspect ratio screen. The Titanium is a light 2.5 pounds, it's a 2 in 1 laptop with a 13.5 inch 3 x 2 aspect ratio screen. It comes with a pen included in the box that attaches magnetically to the side of a laptop. Next up is the carbon, a regular laptop with a 14 inch 16 x 10 aspect ratio screen that weighs a tiny bit more than the Titanium at 2.6 pounds. But it's still very lightweight. And finally, the Yoga Gen 6, which is a larger 2 in 1 laptop with a 14 inch 16 x 10 aspect ratio screen, it is the heaviest of the bunch at 3.1 pounds. But keep in mind, even though it is the heaviest, the MacBook Pro 13 weighs a similar amount with a smaller screen, so I wouldn't consider it that heavy. Let's hit performance. All these laptops can be equipped with either i5s or i7s, but the Nano and the Titanium both use the supposed lower power CPUs, whereas the carbon and the Yoga use regular Ultra Books CPUs. The reason I said supposed is because if you've been watching my channel for a while, you'll know that with current Intel laptops, their performance depends more on how much power the manufacturer chooses to feed into the processor and whether the laptops design can keep the CPU cool and for how long, rather than which exact model processor it is. Let's jump into Geekbench, which tests a variety of common tasks. You can see the Titanium massively underperforms while the X1 Carbon with the i7 processor is the best of the bunch. In Cinebench R23, which tests how the CPU performs under maximum load, it's the same story. Notice that the tiny Nano performs very well in both the CPU tests. By the way, I think I know the issue why the Titanium underperforms. When you look at the max temperatures, the CPU is allowed to hit before reducing performance to keep the processor cool. It seemed the Titanium's max temperature is kept at 89 celsius. The other laptops processors are able to run hotter and therefore faster for longer. Taking a look at graphics performance both times my and in particular fast-strike it reinforces this. The Titanium is last in the X1 Carbon in yoga with the i7 perform the best. Keep in mind the G7 graphics in the i7 processors do have additional graphics execution units and that's helping these laptops perform well in graphics. In PCMark 10, the test standard offers tasks the Titanium now performs well enough but still way below the carbon with the i7 processor and the yoga gen 6. Even though these aren't video editing laptops, you can see that when exporting a 4K video in Premiere Pro, the carbon and the yoga are again in the lead by substantial margin. Those laptops should be good enough for some light video editing. When it comes to temperatures that you'd actually feel during light use like browsing the web or watching a movie, the carbon and surprisingly given how thin it is the Titanium remain very cool to the touch. The nano gets a little warm and the yoga gets noticeably warm which can be a little distracting. Under heavy load though, the nano and the carbon with the i5 processor are the coolest laptops to the touch. When it comes to fan noise, the carbon was pretty much dead silent for most tasks. On the other laptops I did hear the fan going even for light use but to be honest it wasn't loud nor high pitch so not that disturbing but you will hear it. Here are the SSD speeds, the Titanium is a little slower. Alright onto the rest of the laptops. The track pads on the yoga and nano were excellent. The carbons were a mixed bag. One unit's track pad was usable but not enjoyable as it was pretty slippery. The other unit's track pad was outright unusable, way too slippery. If you do buy a carbon and it comes with a bad track pad, get the unit replaced as the track pad in my i5 model was usable. The Titanium's track pad was very challenging to use, it felt cheap and I found it inaccurate. The track pad didn't depress properly and didn't have that satisfying click you'd expect. By the way I don't use the red pointer, I use the track pads. I found that all these laptops having the left and right buttons for the red pointer taking up space at the top of the track pad frustrating as it made the track pad smaller than on competing laptops. Like its track pad, the keyboard in the Titanium also felt very cheap and low travel. Unfortunately all these laptops keyboards felt low travel. The days of awesome super comfy think pad keyboards seems to be unfortunately behind us with the X1 range. If I had to rank the keyboards, it would be the Titanium last. Yoga after that, which does cross the line of being a comfortable keyboard, carbon next as it does feel a bit more classic think pad and then surprisingly the nano's being quite satisfying to use. The displays are all very good. To get started with my tests I first used Windows display scaling to set all laptops to the amount that I was comfortably able to see the most information on screen without needing to squint. My favourite display was the yogas. This 14 inch 16 by 10 aspect ratio screen is excellent. Very bright and very colour accurate. The combination of the yogas resolution, display size and brightness enabled me to see a large amount of content on screen which really matters for productivity. You can see this represented by this graph showing the number of rows in Excel that I was able to see. My next favourite display was again surprisingly the nano's. Even though it's only a small 13 inch display, its matte non glossy screen with just the right amount of pixels is so good. In fact I was able to see the same amount of information on that screen as I'm a much larger yoga which is incredible. That being said, it isn't as colour accurate as that screen. Next would be the titanium. It also has a good screen, but I prefer the 16 by 10 aspect ratio of the other screens versus 3 by 2. The black borders are too large when watching movies on that aspect ratio. I find a 16 by 10 is the sweet spot per seeing a balance of more information when using applications that go down the page, thus being immersed when watching a movie. My least favourite screens by far were the carbons. I tried both the Full HD Plus 400 NET non touch one and the 4K Plus one. The 4K Plus screen was super glossy and reflective, more so than the glossy screen on the yoga. This made it harder to see in bright elit environments. The Full HD Plus screen on the other hand just as in as crisp to look at compared to these other displays, especially for its larger 14 inch size. In fact I saw the least amount of information on screen on that configuration of any of these laptops. When it comes to the chassis, the carbon and nano feel like high quality laptops than the others. They have that signature soft robbery feel that you expect on a think pad. The yoga feels like any other decent quality metallic laptop and the titanium feels cheap. But it has the largest bezels around the screen, especially the chin. None of these laptops have RAM that you can replace, which is unfortunate. But they all have SSDs that you can. Although check which size of the SSD that the laptop uses before ordering one online. For example the titanium uses the shorter form of SSD. All these laptops come equipped with the headphone, mic, combo jack and two USB Thunderbolt 4 ports that both support charging. Unfortunately all the charging ports are on the left side, which means you'll have to run a power cable around the back if your outlet is on the right, which can be annoying. I prefer laptops that have one charging port on either side. The port situation though is a big win for the carbon and the yoga. They also have two USB ports, albeit the slower Gen 1 speeds. Plus they also have an HDMI 2.0 port. Both the yoga and the titanium are two in one so you can easily flip around and use as a tablet. The yoga has a pen that slots into its chassis which is handy as you are less likely to lose it. The titanium comes with a pen that's included in the box that attaches to it via magnets, but it seems to fall off pretty easily. That being said the titanium's pen is larger and more comfortable to write or draw with, but you could always just buy a larger pen for the yoga anyway and have the best of both worlds. Oh and I definitely found the titanium much harder to write on in some modes as it screen wobbles more than the yogas. When it comes to the sound quality from the speakers my favourite is the yoga. It has an excellent immersive sound stage. Its speakers get very loud and they remain really clear. My next favourite is the Nano which gets surprisingly loud and is also very clear. The carbon is next. It's the loudest of the bunch but it's sound stage isn't as immersive as the yogas. And lastly the titanium. Alright let's talk battery life. I left all laptops playing Netflix videos on Wi-Fi, on repeat for almost 4 hours on better battery setting with brightness turned down by 3 notches. Please keep in mind that you will be able to get longer runtimes if you dim the screen further. The titanium and Nano both performed very well. I presume their lower powered processes had something to do with this. The titanium though was a standout but the longest runtimes for the smallest battery. The carbon also performed very well although it has a larger battery. The yoga though was a big disappointment. Yes, perhaps it's bright, high resolution screen had something to do with it. Even at 3 notches down on the brightness it still is at a fairly bright 300 nits. But this is a big drop in battery life. If I had more time I'd do a clean install and retest it to see if there was some rogue program that perhaps was running in the background and using battery. If this is true, this could explain why the yoga felt warmer to the touch than the others. Yet another thing for me to add to the backlog of videos I have to do. Before I wrap I occasionally got this weird screen issue on the carbon and yoga when they were plugged into an external display. Restarting those laptops did fix it and I would assume it is to do with the drivers. But I thought I should mention it anyway. After using all these laptops for two weeks here's where I stand. The titanium's pros are that it's lightweight, super thin, has great battery life and is a 2 in 1. It's cons are that it definitely underperforms the other laptops and feels cheap and I really don't like the keyboard and trackpad. I personally wouldn't buy it. The carbon is the most powerful of the bunch and has exceptionally long battery life for its performance. It also is the quietest and coolest feeling laptop to use. That being said, its screen options are a disappointment. One is super reflective and the other I just don't see enough information on the screen to be competitive with these other laptops. Also, its trackpad isn't the best. That being said, I do feel the carbon is a solid buy. Then there is the yoga which I believe is a very good laptop and the best or round laptop of the bunch. It's got the best screen, it folds into a tablet with an included pen, the sound is excellent and it's plenty powerful. That being said, its battery life was unimpressive. Although as I mentioned, perhaps I had a road program installed and it did feel a little warm to the touch especially in light use. Its biggest condo is its starting price. I personally would only buy it if I got it on one of Lenovo's regular rotating sales much lower than the price I saw it for. Lastly, the Nano. I believe this is the standard device of the bunch. It's just so friggin good and it's so lightweight. It really punches above its weight. I cannot believe I just said that pun. Anyway, the only negatives really are that it doesn't perform quite as well as the bigger carbon and yoga and you will hear the fans occasionally. Well I hope this video helped you choose which of these laptops to get or at least entertain you for a couple of minutes. If it did, you know what to do, smash that subscribe button, hit the thumbs up and the notification bell. I would serve my appreciated and so would my mum. If you'd like early looks at tech I'm covering or just to hear a bit about my life, make sure to follow me on Instagram, Twitter and TikTok links below. As I always say, go do something awesome with your day or in my case night and I will catch you later.

titulo: ThinkPad X1 Carbon Gen 9 Review - The best all round Windows laptop
transcricao: Let's get into it. With me is the newly redesigned Lenovo X1 Carbon 9th Gen, an important laptop. You see outside of Apple's MacBook line, I'd say ThinkPad's are probably one of the most respected lines out there. When you hear ThinkPad, you tend to think, good quality build, great keyboard, upgradability and configurability. I think most people would consider the ThinkPad T-series the quintessential ThinkPad, but with the move to thinner and lighter laptops, I believe it's now this one, the X-series. In my mind, the 14-inch screen size that both the series has is really the perfect size. It's small enough to make the laptop portable that large enough to get some solid work done. In fact, the older X1 Carbon 7th Gen was the number one laptop I was recommending around the $1,000 mark for those looking for lightweight use. Browsing the web, schoolwork, office, emails and even some basic programming. That was until Apple updated the MacBook Air, which is currently the one I've been recommending. Anyway, Lenovo is back with a redesign ThinkPad X1 Carbon with a host of changes, including a new 16x10 aspect ratio screen, which should allow you to see more information for applications that go down the page. By the way, I bought this laptop for myself. Not for power user tasks though, I'm definitely not going to be rendering the video that you're watching now on it, but I was personally excited about its many improvements, so let's see how it turns out. By the way, if you're new here, I'm Josh and I buy and review a lot of laptops and talk tech from the perspective of what it's like to own and use these devices. If at the end of this video, you like what you watched, make sure to smash that subscribe button, hit the thumbs up and the notification bell. Not only does it show your appreciation for the insane amount of work that goes into making these, but it also makes my mother very happy. Now, this review is going to draw from my recent review of the ThinkPad Nano. If you haven't watched that review, please do so, I'll post a link to it in the description below. Alright, let's start with performance as it is very good on this laptop. Side note, the performance profiles of this laptop can be configured from the Windows Power Slider. Now, because I bought this laptop for me, I opted for the model with the iFight processor, not the i7. I did that because I felt the laptop would run a bit cooler, even if it meant sacrificing a little single core performance, as this iFight has a max clock speed of 4.2 GHz compared to the 4.7 GHz of the i7s in the Intel laptops that I'm going to compare it with. So, no surprises that in Geekbench, this laptop is a little behind in single core performance, but still easily good enough in multi core performance, which I personally believe is more important. It's actually the best score on a portable Intel laptop that I've ever recorded. Now, when we turn over to CCINABENCHR23, which maxes out the CPU, the result is also very good. Much faster than the direct Windows competitors, the Dell XPS and the HP Spectre. However, it is still slower than the HP NB14, which has the same CPU. That laptop is quite a bit larger and heavier though. When I ran the torture test on repeat for 10 minutes, you can see that the X1 carbon starts to pull away from its smaller thick Padanono brother. However, it doesn't sustain its performance as well as the NB14. You can see why when we look at PowerDraw, this laptop initially draws 41 watts of power and then settles at 24 watts, which is very good. The NB14 outperforms it, continuously drawing more power, and here are the matching clock speeds. For real world applications, this laptop was amongst the fastest I've tested, including for programming when starting the integrated development environment in Teluguay, compiling and debugging a Java Enterprise Edition project and loading a large MySQL database. In fact, a close friend of mine wanted some help with her R programming assignment. I've been wanting to learn R for quite some time. It's a programming language mainly used for statistical analysis. Anyway, I chose to learn it on this laptop and I found the experience very good. On to video editing. Performance was also very good. Editing on a Premiere Pro 4K video timeline was very smooth and even exporting that 4K video was very fast. For gaming, my fire strike and time spy scores show that this laptop is suitable for lightweight games such as playing League of Legends. In fact, even with the displays greater than the usual resolution of 1920x1200, this laptop had no problems playing that title at all for settings. In fact, it was hitting well over the max 60 frames per second. And by the way, on this test, I forgot to set the laptop's performance to best performance. So I would imagine you can get even more frames than I'm showing on screen. Let's talk about fan noise and heat. For lightweight tasks like browsing the web, watching movies and writing office documents, today I'm introducing a new test to help me measure it. I set up several laptops playing at twitch.tv string for 15 minutes and measured the temperatures that you'd feel on the keyboard deck and the underside of the laptop. What I found was that this laptop was more than 3 degrees Celsius cooler. You will definitely notice this as it makes this laptop more comfortable to use for casual tasks. In fact, this laptop is one of the coolest and quietest that I've ever used when I had it on my laptop. But when we look at the heat generated from the MacBook Pro 1 for the exact same task, it still destroys this laptop. However, the X1 Carbon does cross that bar that you won't be distracted by fueling heat or hearing fan noise while using it. For example, as I walked around the table while this test was running, I could hear fan noise from my Dell XPS and some occasional very loud bursts of fan noise from my HP Spectre 14. In fact, the only time I ever heard the fans going on this laptop was during a Zoom call. And yes, unlike the thing Pagnano, Zoom worked flawlessly on this laptop. Now, when we look at heat and fan noise it produces under heavy load like rendering a video, this laptop does get very warm to the touch and its fan noise is around the middle of the pack. A couple of other performance notes for those who need them. The SSD speed is very good, latency mon results aren't great and Wi-Fi download speeds are excellent. So let's sum up performance. This is one of the best performing thinner light laptops I've ever used and the fact that it runs so cool and quiet for most tasks is just phenomenal. Please keep in mind, my unit only has an i5 processor. It makes me wonder if there may be some more performance to eag out of it with an i7. That being said, it would be nice to have an AMD Ryzen 5000 processor as an option for this laptop. However, realistically, this laptop is totally fast enough. As mentioned, even for programming and some lightweight video editing and gaming will be totally fine. Let's talk battery life next as it's a standout. I easily got over 8 hours with the brightness close to max for casual tasks. This laptop should be able to heat around 10 hours if you turn down the brightness and tweaks and power saving settings. In fact, this is one of those rare laptops that when you check how much battery is left, it's almost always more than you would expect. The laptop's chassis is solidly built. I noticed no worrying screen flex or sharp edges and I could open it with one hand. The laptop is also very light for a 14-inch one at 2.5 pounds which makes it super comfortable to use. The port selection is excellent for a small laptop. Two Thunderbolt 4 ports that both support charging, two handy USB-A ports and an HDMI 2.0 port. I would have liked to see a Thunderbolt port on each side so I don't have to run a charging cable around the back if the outlet is on the other side. Overall, it's a good port selection. The speakers are downward facing even though the grills on either side of the keyboard would make you think otherwise. My guess is that these are for airflow. Regardless, the speakers get plenty loud and have good stereo separation. That being said, these speakers are good but definitely not at the level of the MacBook Pro 13 M1 which has a much greater range to the sound especially when it comes to bass reproduction. Those speakers just hit you with their power. This laptop was one of the easiest to open I've ever seen. Just five screws that stay in place even when I'm screwed so you won't lose them. Looking inside the laptop you can see the dual fans, replaceable SSD and it even looks like a spot for a second small form factor M.2 expansion card. The battery is a large 57 watt hour one which helps explain the long run times. Unfortunately RAM is sold at low. For the display I have the 400-net low power 1920x1200 resolution nontouch one. The display is pretty good on paper and not bad in real life. It's bright, colour accurate enough, has good contrast and it isn't reflective. But for the price range it isn't one of my favourite screens. Predominantly due to the amount of information I could comfortably see on it. I personally find when buying a laptop one of the most important things is how much info you can see on the screen. The more information I see, the more productive I am. Now the amount of information I can comfortably see on a laptop without having to squint is a combination of many factors. Getting some that this screen does very well. It's bright, it isn't reflective and it's a large 14 inch one. But for the size of the panel, I don't find the resolution high enough. I found that I could only comfortably run the screen at 125% window scaling before things became too small for me to see properly. When you do the math, that means I'm seeing an equivalent of 960 pixels vertically. This is less information than what I was able to comfortably see on my smaller 13 inch think pad nano. That laptop has a better resolution for its screen size and on it I never felt like I was seeing pixels whereas on this one I feel like I am at that window scaling setting. It is a disappointment as I was hoping to take better advantage of the 14 inch screen. Good news though, there is apparently a higher resolution but still low power panel coming for it which sounds very promising so make sure you're subscribed with the notification bell clicked as I will absolutely be getting that one when it comes out. Now before we move on, I notice no PWM flickering used to lower the brightness or backlight bleed in my model. The keyboard is good enough but it's definitely not my favourite. It's unfortunate because the impads used to have the most comfortable keyboards out there. This year they've gone with a lower travel one and although some low travel keyboards, like the one in the Dell XPS 931O still feel great, this one bottoms out quickly. The click though is soft and it does have that distinctive thing pad feel to it but you will notice that lack of travel. In fact even the smaller thinkpad nano has a more comfortable keyboard. One positive thing about it though is it is relatively quiet to use so it's not going to be overly disturbing if you're typing in a meeting. Thinkpads do have the function and control key swap from typical keyboards which can be frustrating. A viewer pointed out that if you download the updated Lenovo commercial vantage software from the window store, you will be able to swap these keys back easily without having to restart the laptop to do it in the BIOS. Seriously guys, I learned so much from your comments and it helps me become a better reviewer. Overall I'd say that this keyboard isn't above average, it's more comfortable than the one in Apple's MacBooks but not as comfortable as the one in the Dell XPS or the HB Spectre. The new larger trackpad is a welcome improvement from the older version which I found too small. It does feel a bit slippery though compared to the trackpad on the X1 nano which I like better. Once I turned down the trackpad speed it was perfectly usable but it isn't as good as the trackpad in the ASUS G15 or Apple's MacBooks. And here's how the webcam looks and sounds in excellent lighting additions. It does have a privacy filter at the top. This laptop also has Windows Hello facial recognition as well as a fingerprint reader in the power button which both worked well. A lot of people seem to be enjoying my Linux testing so after reading comments I decided to extend the tests. Ubuntu 20.04 revision 2 worked excellent straight out of the box. Keyboard, trackpad, function keys, audio, wifi all worked well. I also tested the webcam and ran a video while closing the laptops lid to test whether it would go to sleep. Both worked as expected. In terms of stability, the only issue I noticed in the entire time I used this laptop was the display issue that you see on screen. It only happened once when I was plugged into an external monitor. I unplugged the laptop, restarted it and re-plugged it in and all was good. Lastly, price. This laptop is not cheap. I bought my config with 16GB RAM and a 512GB SSD for around $1900 USD. This is too expensive. I could buy the MacBook Pro 13 M1 with 16GB RAM and a 512GB SSD for less. Lenovo does tend to have some massive rotating sales that drops some config substantially in price. Take a look at this thing Pannano's sale I found. Hopefully the price doesn't stay this high. Heck, one of the reasons I was recommending the older X1 Carbon so much was because you could buy them for around $1,000 USD. So this leads me into who should buy this laptop. This is the perfect laptop for casual users browsing the web, writing emails, doing office work and students. Plus, it's got plenty of grant for programming, some simple 4K video editing and eSports gaming. That being said, those who are doing more intensive programming video editing or triple A gaming should look elsewhere and obviously this is not a budget laptop. The X1 Carbon is definitely more comfortable for use than most other Windows laptops out there, including the Dell XPS, HBNV14 or the HB Spectre 14. That's because it's lightweight, powerful, has great battery life and runs incredibly cool to the touch as well as being quiet. Most Windows laptops fail on at least one of these. If you do want more power in a portable Windows laptop though, I look at the extremely hard to find iDARPAD Slim 7 Pro with Ryzen 5000. That laptop not only will outperform this one in CPU tasks especially multicore but it has a better screen. You will have to deal with a less comfortable keyboard though shorter battery life and slightly less powerful graphics. Overall, the X1 Carbon is a really good all-round laptop that you just aren't going to have any issues with, which honestly is what a lot of people have been waiting to hear. So I recommend it. Anyway, that's all for today folks, a bit of a long review but this is an important laptop. Hope you enjoyed it. If you did, make sure to smash that subscribe button, hit the thumbs up and the notification bell. I would certainly appreciate it and as mentioned, so would my mother. Till next time, go do something awesome with your day and I will catch you later.

titulo: HP Envy 15 - The BEST Video Editing Laptop Under $2,000
transcricao: Alright tech family, I wanted to hop on today to talk about the HBNV15 as I believe it is one of the best video editing laptops that money can buy. In fact, I've only your time, so I'm just going to jump to the conclusion and say it is the best video editing laptop that you can buy under $2,000. Now, this is going to be a very unusual review for me because it's going to be quite brief. This laptop has been out for some time and a lot of laptop reviewers have already covered in depth. So, I'm going to quickly go over some performance results to set the stage, then I'm going to just jump straight into my personal experience using the laptop. The laptop arrived over a month ago, but I deprioritized reviewing it because I felt new guys would be more interested in me covering the launch of Intel's new 11-gen processors rather than this laptop, which had been reviewed a lot before. However, since it is now the most important buying season of the year and this laptop has received a lot of positive reviews, I wanted to try it for myself to see just how good or bad it was. So, I opened it up and gave it a go. Straight away, I saw that it was a bit big and bulky for most students or casual users to carry around, plus it doesn't support U.S. PC charging, which isn't that convenient. My model with the 1650 Ti and the somewhat mushy keyboard was also not ideal for gaming, but I quickly noticed that for video editing, this laptop was a dream, and so I edited my portion of the last two videos on it. The reason I say my portion is because I have a video editor and we edit collaboratively together. I like to do the final edit and explore the videos myself because I have a particular artistic vision that I want to achieve. At the end of the day, this laptop performs so well as a video editing laptop that I felt it important to give you my thoughts on it, and heck, that's why a lot of you watch this channel to begin with, to know information that goes beyond the benchmarks. What is it like to actually own and use the device? Since I felt this laptop really targets video editors, I'm going to compare it with the laptop I use for my video editing, my MacBook Pro 16, and another popular video editing laptop, the Dell XPS 15. By the way, I have the 10750H model with a 6-core processor, 1650 Ti graphics, the gorgeous 4K OLED screen, 32GB RAM and a 1TB SSD. Let's go over performance as there are some important things here to be aware of. I did my tests on HP's default mode and performance mode. For Geekbench, the laptop performs excellently in both single core and multi core. You can see it beating out its more expensive competitor at the Dell XPS 15, 9500. In Cinebench, which maxes out the CPU, you can see that it performs better than the 15-inch Dell XPS. What's really good here is even on the default mode, where the HP NV runs pretty quietly, it performs almost as well as the XPS on its fastest ultra-performance mode. As you can see though, my MacBook Pro 16 with its 8-core CPU has the edge as the 6-core CPU in my NV just can't catch it. Turning to temperatures that you would actually feel when the laptops under load, this is where you see the NV starting to shine. Take a look at how low the temperatures are on the NV. Look at the temperature on the keyboard deck when running Cinebench. That is outstanding. Honestly, even when I edited a video editing it for over an hour, I did notice it a little warm, but it still felt cooler to the touch than my MacBook Pro 16 and the XPS 15. Now, looking at the CPU temperatures went under load, not bad at all. These temps are as good as you'll get on an Intel CPU. Here is fan noise. You can see that on performance mode it gets quite loud, but on default mode it isn't too bad. When you look at power draw, you can see that in both modes it draws well over 90 watts and then quickly drops to 50 watts on performance and a lower 37 watts on the default mode. Moral of the story is this. This laptop performs really well, and in the default mode it runs pretty cool to the touch and the fans aren't that loud for the performance you're getting out of it. I personally would take that trade off and run the laptop in the default mode. I will say this, I like how HP gives you the owner the choice of how you want to run the laptop. The only thing that I'll add is even right now the fans are on. I can hear them. I'm not sure if it's picking up in the mic. They're not that loud, but they are on. Alright, in real world usage I had one of the best video editing experiences I've ever had when cutting through footage on the timeline, even on one of my most complex 4K video projects with multiple cameras and tons of B-roll and effects. Just a note, I did still get drop frames when playing back at 4K resolution, but it had no problems with half resolution, which is totally fine. Overall, it was smoother than on my MacBook Pro 16 and pretty much any other laptop I've used. However, when I went to export it, it was a decent amount slower than on my MacBook Pro 16. Results on screen. Please keep in mind that I have the lower end 1650 Ti GPU in this unit. When I observed its usage when exporting, it was hitting 100%. So I'd assume that if I had the much more powerful 1660 Ti or 2060 GPU in here, it would export more competitively against the MacBook Pro 16. By the way, I did have some odd Premiere Pro errors when the export would sometimes fail. I found that restarting Premiere Pro fixed this, so my assumption is it's something to do with mind-store. Alright, so hopefully you see that this laptop is very powerful and runs relatively cool and quiet on the default mode. Let's now talk about some things that I noticed when editing off it, and how my experience compares to the MacBook Pro 16. Overall, you can definitely feel the drop in build quality of this laptop, this chassis definitely doesn't feel as well built. I also found the silver model scratch fairly easily, I got two rather large scratches on it, so if you buy this machine, I'd put a case or skin on it straight away. The keyboard feels mushy compared to how precise the MacBook Pro 16 feels. Also, I don't like the Envy's layout, I made a lot of mistakes by accidentally pressing the keys from the additional row on the far right that aren't normally there. I would assume that if this was my only laptop, I'd probably get used to that over time. The trackpad also lacked accuracy compared to the MacBook Pro 16. By the way, my Dell XPS 9500 was more in line with the MacBook Pro 16 in terms of how it felt. I eat a more premium experience. When it comes to the display though, the 4K OLED panel in the Envy is absolutely excellent. Also special note here about something iPhone super handy. If you're plugging this laptop into an external monitor with an IPS panel which is most of them, it's great to have both types of panels to view the video you're editing on. IPS which is in most computers, and OLED which is often in phones and TVs. This allows you to ensure your content looks just right on both types of displays. I previously posted videos that look really good on one, but not on another. So this is super handy. That being said, I still prefer the display of the MacBook Pro 16. I really find that that size and 16x10 aspect ratio more useful for productivity tasks. By the way, you may notice in the B-roll that the Envy 15 OLED has a display that is very reflective. This panel gets quite bright and when using it you don't really notice the reflections. When it comes to the speakers, the MacBook Pro 16 wipes the floor with the Envy. The Envy isn't bad, but the MacBook Pros are just on another level. Port-wise, the Envy does have USB-A ports which is super helpful, but for some reason it has a microSD card reader rather than full size one. Why? One thing I really don't like is the Envy can't be charged via USB-C. This means you start carrying around the power brick which reduces the portability of the laptop. The power brick though isn't that large, but it's still substantially larger than some USB-C charges that would provide adequate power for most everyday tasks like browsing the web. One of the best things though about the Envy is that it is upgradable. Yes, both RAM slots are accessible and there are two M.2 slots for storage. Awesome. Overall though, would I personally buy the HP Envy over the MacBook Pro 16 for video editing? No, I would not. The MacBook Pro 16 is a higher quality device. Well, why do I give this laptop such a resounding recommendation? Because you can't purchase a MacBook Pro 16 with similar specs anywhere near the price of the Envy. Take a look. There are two configurations of the Envy that I recommend for video editing. A budget video editing config with a 6-core processor, 6-inch RAM and a 1650 Ti. And a high performance one with the same 6-core processor, however, with 32-inch RAM and the more powerful 1660 Ti. I wouldn't bother with the A-core processor as it adds around $450 USD to the price and even with the decent cooling in this laptop, a data will perform substantially better to justify that price difference. Anyway, check out the price of the Dell XPS and the MacBook Pro 16. The HP Envy is just so much cheaper. Seriously, when I think about other laptops that you can edit videos on in the sub-$2,000 price range, the only laptops that spring to mind are gaming laptops like the Aero 15, which has more annoying fans, especially for light-tars and it has coil-wind. Or the HP Omen and the Lenovo Legion, both with a bigger bulkier laptops. Honestly, the HP Envy 15 really is the laptop to buy if you are focused on editing videos and have a budget of less than $2,000. I've started installing sound outening but I've got a lot more to go. Anyway, let's talk about the HBNV13 with AMD. This laptop was sent to me by HP. They gave me no guidance on what to say and have not reviewed this video. I'm probably not going to give this preface in front of future reviews and tech that companies send me because I would never sacrifice my integrity just because a manufacturer wants me to say certain things. Believe me, these companies are sending me these devices at their own risk. Anyway, at the time of creating this video, I couldn't find this exact model for sale. My one has a Ryzen 4500 new processor 8GB RAM and the 400nit brightness screen. That being said, Best Buy has a very similar model which apparently also has the 400nit screen. The only difference is there one has the more powerful 8-core processor. I'll link it in the description below. By the way, I'm Josh and I buy and review a lot of laptops and talk tech from the perspective of what it's like to own and use these devices. If at the end of this video, you like what you watched, don't forget to smash that subscribe button, hit the thumbs up and the notification bell. It shows your appreciation for the insane amount of work that goes into making these. Before we get back to the laptop, I just want to say I'm reading all your comments and I hear you about my head nodding while I'm talking. It's distracting and I'm definitely working on it. Alright, let's hit performance first. HP appears to have prioritized this laptop feeling cool to the touch when running any task, including intensive ones like gaming and productivity. This makes it a very comfortable laptop to use. The downside is the way they seem to over-achieve this. The laptop's power is limited to drawing 25 watts, which is lower than the other AMD 4000 series laptops that I've tested. Also, they run the fans quite regularly to call the laptop. Although this laptop performs well compared to laptops with Intel's 10th Gen processor, it performs worse than other laptops with the same AMD processor that I've tested. The Geekbench results tell the same story as Cinebench. I personally prefer the sacrifice they have made to get this laptop to run comfortably cool to the touch, especially as this device is not targeting power users. However, if you are looking for the most power out of an AMD Ryzen laptop, this isn't the one to get. By the way, HP has a command center app that has several options to control performance. Recommended, which appears to quickly cap the laptop at a lower 15 watts of power for a lot less fan noise, not no fan noise, and then performance, which has the laptop run at 25 watts of power for more fan noise. By the way, even though I said you do hear the fans a lot on this machine, it isn't as bad as many laptops that I've tested as the fan noise is not high pitched. Full casual and eSports gaming that is not intensive, the laptop performed pretty well. In League of Legends, I was able to get an excellent 80-90 frames per second at 1920 by 1080 on medium settings, which is very playable, and the keyboard deck was a comfortable 39 Celsius. Here are my times by and fire strike scores. The SSD that the laptop comes with has disappointing performance. I normally expect to see ASSSD scores of around 3000+. The RAM is in dual channel mode, which is good, but make sure you buy it with the RAM you need as it is soldered. The Wi-Fi 6 underperformed other devices that I have. Audio latency results were very good, even when I ran numerous applications in the background. When it comes to upgradability, this laptop is brutal to get inside of. There are screws below the rubber foot at the back, and you know once you rip that off, you'll never get it properly back on. Even when you do take those screws out, I could not pry open the laptop, even with a spludging kit without damaging it. Let's talk about the display. It's the best in any budget laptop that I've used to date, period. I have the 400-in version, and it has good color accuracy and excellent brightness. The glossy touch panel on top makes everything look super sharp. I had no dead pixels, no noticeable backlight bleed, and no PWM flickering when you lower the brightness. The device can fold into a tablet, which is a nice touch for such a small device like this. Please be careful when buying this laptop. It comes with several different display options. I would absolutely avoid the 250-net panel. It is too dim for most users, you'll find yourself squinting. Now, even though this is a good display, I find most 13.3 inch screens too small for productivity work, and I would avoid them if you work with lots of spreadsheets, or are a software developer or video editor. Let me explain. On a 13-inch screen with a resolution of 1920 by 1080 pixels like this one, if I run Windows scaling at 100% everything looks too small as information is compressed across the small display. I find I need to zoom in and run it at 125% scaling. This results in seeing less information. When doing heavy productivity work like using large spreadsheets or coding, there is a lot of information you need to see, and you just don't see enough. Even when writing a document in Word, I only see about half a page, which means I have to scroll a lot. By the way, that's why people are into screens with aspect ratios such as 16 by 10 or 3 by 2, as they allow you to see more vertical information. These aspect ratios do help people who are using Word or browsing the web, as those apps don't really use the full horizontal space, but they don't really help coders, video editors, or data analysts. Their applications really adapt well to any screen aspect ratio, and those people just need more screen real estate. Take a look at how much code I would see in IntelliJ, the integrated development environment, with 125% scaling. Not a lot. Yes, of course, I can see more by making my code window full screen, but then I've got to constantly switch to access the other information that I no longer see. Let's cut the crap. I believe a 13.3 screen is totally fine for casual users browsing the web or students that aren't studying things like financial analysis or programming. It's also a great option if you plan to use it with an external monitor when doing those kind of tasks, as you get the best of both worlds, portability and productivity. However, if you are planning to use this laptops display as your only one for the tasks I mentioned, I'd strongly recommend you look at a laptop with a minimum screen size of 14 inches and 1920 resolution. That should enable you to run at 100% scaling and see more information. My only exception to this is the 13 inch MacBook Pro. It has a high fidelity 16 by 10 retina screen, which means you can make out slightly smaller fonts more easily and have more vertical real estate. Plus, I personally find Mac OS and its apps by default are better optimised for smaller screens. Onto the chassis, it feels very premium and looks fantastic with small bezels and no sharp edges. Although personally, I'm not the huge fan of the colour, it looks better than I thought it would. The screen hinge is tight enough that it doesn't fall back when touching it, which used to happen on some of the older HP convertibles. There is some screen flex though, and the laptop does pick up fingerprints, but they aren't too hard to clean off. Here is what the laptop weighs, and now with the included charger. The keyboard is excellent. Amongst the best I've used, Apple Key Travel, no surprises in the layout, good contrast between the keys and the backlight. Also, I love how they are dedicated buttons to the stable that webcam and mic, great for zoom calls. Plus, they have a handy light on the keyboard that indicates when you have one of those functions enabled. There is no Windows IR, hello camera, but it does have a fingerprint reader, however, it didn't work the best for me. The Windows Precision Trackpad is quite good and substantially better than the horrid synaptic trackpad in the older HP laptops. It also doesn't depress much in the corners like the bad Dell XPS ones. The laptop has a good enough selection of ports that you won't frequently need to reach for a dongle. It has two USB ports, one USB-C port and a microSD card reader. It comes with a barrel pin charger, but you can also use a USB-C charger, which is great as it gives you convenience to free up that USB-C port, but also usually abundance of USB-C charges available. Unfortunately, both charging cable reports are on the left side, so if your outlet is on the right, you will have to run the cable around the back, which could get in the way of a mouse if you are right-handed. Sorry, no thunderbolt here or USB-4, but HP does claim the USB-C ports are ports the faster 10GB connection, which is nice, even though the USB-A ports are the slower ones, Overall, the ports on this laptop match my recommended use case for the laptop. It's a great, very portable computer that, say, you're out on the go and want to charge up from someone else's USB-C charger you can, or take photos using a microSD card and then view them on the laptop. Sound quality is pretty good and it gets quite loud. Unfortunately, the speakers are underneath and downward facing. You will lose a lot of volume if something blocks these. For example, you use the laptop on a blanket on your lap. The webcam is the usual garbage. Here's how it looks and sounds in excellent lighting conditions. It's odd that they added those custom keyboard buttons for video calls, but still have a crap webcam in it. Battery life was really good. I found that when watching YouTube and writing this script, the battery drained between, say, 10% to 18% per hour with the screen at close to max brightness. I think you should easily be able to get 8 hours or more if you lower the brightness. Lastly, the laptop was very stable and never crashed. Let's wrap up. After using this laptop as my daily driver for well over a week, I feel confident in saying that this is an absolutely excellent laptop. This is the first non-gaming Ryzen 4000 laptop that really gets the basics right without any major compromises. It feels incredibly premium, it has a great screen, excellent keyboard, doesn't get too hot to the touch and handles any lightweight task I could throw at it with ease. And at the price point of the similar best by model of around 800 US dollars, it is the best deal I've seen in this price range. I mean, let's compare it to other laptops that I've tested with a similar price. It's got a substantially better display than the Lenovo iDead5s. It has a backlit keyboard and webcam, which the Redmi book doesn't. You can actually see the keys when the backlight is on, unlike the Aces Nbook 14. Up until now, I've been telling you to buy an X1 carbon if you are shopping around the 800 to say $1300 US dollar price range. I am now going to be telling you to buy this laptop instead, plus perhaps an external monitor, keyboard and mouse to go with it. This leads me to the most important thing, who should buy this laptop? Because of the small 13.3 inch screen, this is a great laptop for those who are doing extremely casual tasks like browsing the way of watching movies, responding to emails, very basic say learning to code. It's also an excellent second device to complement a less mobile desktop or gaming laptop. However, if you pair it with an external monitor, it really opens this laptop up as an excellent option for most office workers, for example, those using a lot of spreadsheets and of course software developers. Please note, for the software developers out there, I would try to get the 8 core version of this laptop with at least 16GB of RAM if you can afford it. You will be able to code off the config I have, but 16GB would give you more flexibility and longevity. If you are a video editor or looking to play AAA games, this is not the laptop for you. The graphics power in it simply isn't good enough. Well, that's all for today folks. If you like this video, you know what to do. Smash that subscribe button, click the thumbs up and the notification bell. I would certainly appreciate it. Also, if you want to show a little extra support, I do have Patreon, which definitely could use some love. By the way, I tend to post draft versions of my reviews a little earlier for those supporters. Also, you can follow me on Instagram and Twitter for a little more behind the scenes coverage. Link below. Anyway, till next time, I will catch you later.
